items.title: The boundary problem in agentic AI is a platform problem
items.summary: An autonomous agent will do exactly what its tools let it do, and no more. This sounds like a constraint. In practice it is the whole risk, because the set of things an agent’s tools let it do is almost never the set anyone deliberately chose. It is the set that accumulated. A tool added for one workflow stays available for every workflow. A credential scoped for a demo survives into production. A delegation added to unblock a Friday deploy becomes a permanent edge in the graph. Nobody decides to give the agent that reach. There was never a moment where reach was decided at all. This is the pattern worth naming. It is not a bug in any particular agent framework and it will not be fixed by a better prompt. Across enough deployments the same shape recurs: authority is granted incrementally, locally, and invisibly, and the system’s actual power drifts steadily away from anyone’s model of what it should be able to do. The agents behave. The boundaries erode anyway. By the time someone asks “wait, can it do that?”, the honest answer is usually “it could for weeks, and we only noticed now.” The instinct is to treat this as a governance failure and answer with process and review boards. That instinct aims at the wrong layer. Process governs the decisions humans make. This problem is largely about the decisions nobody makes, the capabilities that arrive without a decision, and you cannot review a class of change that never surfaces as a change. What is needed is not more vigilance over the agent. It is a substrate that holds the line whether or not anyone is watching. Why the agent cannot hold its own boundary The tempting shortcut is to make the agent responsible for its own limits: tell it in its instructions what it may and may not do, and give it a sense of its own scope. This fails structurally, and the failure looks like success right up until it doesn’t. An agent’s output is a probability distribution over next actions, conditioned on context. It is not a guarantee. Most of the time the most probable action is the appropriate one, which is exactly what makes agents useful and exactly what makes them dangerous to trust. A boundary that holds ninety-nine times and yields on the hundredth is not a boundary; it is a strong suggestion with a failure rate. And the conditions that push an agent toward the edge of its instructions, novel inputs, adversarial phrasing, unusual state, are precisely the conditions where the boundary matters most and where probabilistic adherence is weakest. You rely on the mechanism least when you need it most. Underneath the reliability problem sits a harder one. Even a perfectly compliant agent, one that always did exactly what its instructions said, would still have whatever authority its tools and credentials actually grant. The instruction is a statement of intent. The tool binding is a statement of capability. When those two disagree, capability wins, because capability is what executes. An agent instructed not to move money, but holding a tool that moves money, is one clever prompt or one confused reasoning step away from moving money. The gap between intended scope and granted capability is the entire attack surface, and no amount of instruction closes it, because instruction and capability live in different layers and only one of them runs. So the boundary has to live where capability lives. Not in the agent’s reasoning, but in the infrastructure that decides what the agent’s reasoning is able to reach. Bounded autonomy is not a property of the agent. It is a property of the platform the agent runs on. The safe operating model Once the boundary belongs to the platform, the problem stops being novel. The industry has spent fifteen years learning to bound what a workload can do, because a microservice is also software that will do whatever its identity, network access, and permissions allow. We built a discipline around not trusting a workload to police itself. An agent is a workload. It is an unusually capable workload with a non-deterministic control loop, but the machinery that bounds workloads applies to it directly. The Safe Operating Model organizes that machinery as concentric rings of least privilege. Each ring binds one question about the agent, and each outer ring depends on the one inside it. The order is not decorative. Reach cannot be enforced without knowing what is connecting; capability cannot be enforced without knowing what is acting. Identity is the center because every other control resolves against it. The core: Identity Identity comes first because every other control depends on knowing what is acting. A workload identity standard issues each agent and each tool server a short-lived, attested credential. The platform no longer takes an agent’s word for what it is; it verifies. Every downstream decision, every reach check, every capability check, keys off this verified identity rather than a bearer token that can leak or be replayed. Get this wrong and the rest is built on sand. Get it right and the boundary has something real to attach to. Everything outward from here is an elaboration of a single question the core has already answered: what, exactly, is this. Ring 1: Reach With identity established, the first thing to bound is reach, meaning what the agent is permitted to connect to. A service mesh enforces this on the verified identity, per connection, independent of network topology. The agent may talk to the specific peers its work requires and to nothing else, and nothing else is the default rather than an afterthought. When an agent tries to reach a service it has no declared relationship with, the connection is refused before it opens. This is where the drift problem first meets a wall. A new edge in the agent’s reach cannot appear quietly at runtime, because reach is declared, and a change to a declaration is visible, reviewable, and attributable. The graph cannot grow in the dark. The accumulation that defined the original problem, one more connection, one more integration, no single one of them a decision, becomes a series of changes that each have to be made on purpose. Ring 2: Capability Reach controls who the agent can talk to. Capability controls what it can actually do, and this is where an agent’s autonomy cashes out: which tools it may invoke, and what it may do to the system. Two enforcement points matter, and they answer two different questions. The first is admission, which governs what capabilities the agent is allowed to hold. When the object that defines an agent’s permitted tools is a declarative resource in the cluster, policy can reject any attempt to bind a tool that was never approved, at the moment of the attempt, before the binding exists. An agent cannot acquire a capability that policy has not sanctioned, because the acquisition itself is what gets denied. A tool nobody reviewed cannot enter the system through the back door of an agent quietly adding it. The second is the call path, which governs what the agent may do with the capabilities it holds. Even among sanctioned tools, a gateway can authorize each individual invocation against the agent’s identity, so that a tool being present and reachable is not the same as a tool being callable. Ask for a tool outside the permitted set and the answer is a refusal, and the tool does not even appear in what the agent can see. Capability becomes something granted per action rather than something latent and waiting to be misused. Holding a tool and being allowed to use it, in a given moment, for a given task, are separated on purpose. The keystone One control sits above the rings and makes them coherent, and it is the one most easily forgotten. Every boundary described so far is expressed as configuration. Identity registrations, mesh authorizations, admission policies, tool allow-lists, all of it is declarative state. Which raises the obvious question: what stops the agent from changing that state? An agent that can edit its own capability definition, or relax the policy that binds it, or grant itself a role, has no real boundary at all, only a boundary it is permitted to remove. So the load-bearing rule, the one that makes bounded autonomy actually bounded, is that the agent’s own identity is denied any ability to modify the objects that define its authority. It can act within its bounds. It cannot rewrite them. Changing what an agent is allowed to do is reserved for a reviewed change to version-controlled configuration, made by a human or a pipeline, never by the agent at runtime. This is what converts a set of controls into a boundary the agent cannot dissolve from the inside, and it is why the model is a set of rings rather than a checklist. The keystone holds the rings closed. Ring 3: Data The outermost ring bounds which records the agent may see, and it is worth being honest about where it lives. Data scope is enforced at the data plane, by the systems that hold the data, rather than by the mesh or the admission controller. But it is not separate from the model, because the enforcement point authorizes against the same verified identity the core established. The rings make data governance possible even though they do not implement it: the identity that proves what the agent is becomes the key the data layer checks. Reach and capability keep the agent away from data sources it should never touch; the data plane decides, within the sources it may touch, which rows are its business. The deterministic spine None of this argues against agent autonomy. It argues about where autonomy belongs. The useful frame is a deterministic spine with non-deterministic execution hanging off it. The spine is the part of the system that must be repeatable, auditable, and correct: the workflow that owns the regulated process, the state, the approvals, the record of who did what and when. That belongs to deterministic infrastructure, durable workflow engines and version-controlled policy, the kind of software that fails the same way every time and leaves a trail. The agent lives inside that spine, in the places where judgment is genuinely valuable: interpreting a document, weighing a signal, drafting a recommendation. It does real cognitive work. It does not own the outcome. In a regulated workflow this is not stylistic. Consider loan origination. The agent can read the application, pull the relevant signals, weigh the risk, and produce a recommendation with its reasoning attached. What it must not do is approve the loan, price it outside policy, or move the funds. Those are deterministic gates and human decisions, and the platform is what keeps them deterministic. The most robust expression of this has the agent emit a proposed change, a draft, a recommendation, a pull request against desired state, which a human reviews and a pipeline applies. Approval stops being a step the agent can talk its way past and becomes a property of the system: the agent has no path to the outcome except through a gate it does not control. This is also what makes the arrangement auditable in the way regulation actually requires. When identity is verified, reach is declared, capability is granted per action, and outcomes flow through reviewed changes, the system produces evidence as a byproduct of operating. You do not reconstruct what the agent was allowed to do; the platform recorded it. You do not trust an after-the-fact account; the boundary left a trail. Provenance that falls out of enforcement is worth more than any assurance an agent could give about its own conduct. What this asks us to build The argument leads somewhere concrete, and it is the opposite of building agent-specific security from scratch. The mature cloud native stack already contains what the Safe Operating Model needs, and the work ahead is integration and rigor rather than invention. Workload identity for agents. Mesh-enforced reach on that identity. Policy-as-code at admission for capability. Per-call authorization at the tool boundary. Version-controlled configuration as the only path to changing any of it. And the discipline to keep the agent out of its own guardrails. These are engineering commitments, and every one of them has a production-grade project behind it today. What is genuinely new is small and specific: expressing an agent’s identity and its permitted capabilities as first-class declarative objects, and enforcing the per-tool authorization that agent-to-tool protocols introduced. That surface is young and moving quickly. But it is a thin new layer on a deep and stable foundation, not a green field. The people who will build trustworthy agentic systems are not the ones searching for a new security paradigm. They are the ones who recognize that an agent is a workload, that workloads have always needed bounding, and that the platform is where bounding has always belonged. The boundary will not come from the agent. It was never going to. Agents are built to explore the space of possible actions, which is exactly why something other than the agent has to decide the shape of that space. Draw the boundary in the platform, make it the default, and let the rings hold it. That is not a limitation on what agentic AI can become. It is the precondition for letting it become anything we can safely rely on. At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 in Salt Lake City, William Rizzo and Kasper Nissen will take these principles from architecture to implementation, exploring how cloud native technologies and projects can be combined to deliver the platform capabilities required to securely govern, observe and operate agentic systems in regulated enterprises. “ Verticalizing Platform Intelligence for Regulated Domains. ”

items.title: ISC2 Launches New AI Security Certification as Cyber Skills Demands Grow
items.summary: As artificial intelligence becomes more widely adopted, cybersecurity professionals are facing growing pressure to develop new skills, understand emerging risks and keep pace with technologies that are changing faster than traditional training programmes can respond. Speaking to IT Security Guru , Matthew Piddington from ISC2 discussed the organisation’s plans to introduce its first dedicated AI security certification, alongside the wider challenges facing the cybersecurity profession. ISC2 is a global not-for-profit organisation representing approximately 270,000 cybersecurity professionals . It provides professional development opportunities and nine certifications, including the internationally recognised Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP) qualification. A New Certification for AI Security One of ISC2’s biggest priorities has been developing a dedicated certification focused on AI security. More than 7,000 volunteers from around the world are currently helping to shape the certification, including defining the examination content, relevant job roles and the knowledge professionals will need to demonstrate. According to Piddington, the initiative responds to growing demand from both cybersecurity and AI professionals for clearer governance and recognised standards around AI security. ISC2 hopes the qualification will eventually achieve the same level of industry recognition as CISSP, which has been established for approximately 30 years. The organisation is targeting the first beta examinations for the first quarter of 2027, with a wider rollout planned from April onwards. Cyber Warfare, AI and Quantum Computing Beyond certification, Matthew highlighted several issues keeping cybersecurity professionals on alert. Geopolitical tensions remain a significant concern, particularly as cyber warfare becomes an increasingly important consideration during periods of international conflict. Security teams must remain prepared for vulnerabilities being exploited, regardless of the sectors in which they operate. AI is creating another challenge. Its rapid adoption is introducing new security risks, while the pace of technological development is making it difficult for organisations and professionals to keep up. Looking further ahead, ISC2 is also considering the implications of quantum computing and the skills cybersecurity professionals will need to address future threats. For Matthew, ensuring the industry has the right expertise is essential to building a safer digital future. Watch the full interview to hear more about ISC2’s AI security certification, the changing cybersecurity skills landscape and the threats shaping the profession’s future.

items.title: State of Ad Fraud 2026: 52% of Schemes Use AI as Cloaking Loses Ground to iOS Exploits and Messenger Phishing
items.summary: The ad fraud landscape changed sharply in 2026. That is the central finding of the State of Ad Fraud 2026: ADEX Trust & Safety Report , published by anti-fraud platform ADEX . The report analyzes January–September 2026 moderation and verification data from eight ad platforms, covering 1.2 million campaigns and 4.9 million creatives. Below are the key findings. Key Findings at a Glance 52% of distinct fraud schemes showed AI-generated or AI-assisted assets. 64% of AI-involved schemes used bots that pass as human visitors. 53% of AI-involved schemes used cloned brands and fake endorsements. 11% of AI-involved schemes used deepfakes. About one-third of rejections were linked to infected domains, which became the top rejection reason from Q2 onward. 6% of Q3 rejections were prize and bonus scareware (“You won a smartphone”), which emerged as its own category that quarter. What Moved in 2026 According to ADEX, the clearest year-on-year shift is in why platforms suspend advertisers. Metric 2025 / Q1 2026 Q3 2026 Cloaking (share of suspensions) ~75% ~45% Malicious iOS scripts (share of suspensions) Not tracked ~20% Copyright (share of rejections) 8% 21% Region-restricted content (share of rejections) 5% 11% Adult content (share of rejections) 42% 14% Cloaking remains the top suspension reason, but it now shares the list with two newer threats: malicious iOS scripts and messenger-based phishing on services such as WhatsApp and Telegram. In those messenger schemes, the persuasion happens in the chat itself. ADEX notes that language models let a single operator run hundreds of believable conversations in any language. Quality Over Quantity ADEX reports that the number of rejected or blocked campaigns fell by roughly a third after Q1. The report says this does not signal a quieter market. Operators shifted from mass submissions to fewer, better-built campaigns. “One well-made scam with a cloned brand page does more damage than a hundred crude ones,” said Sergey Martianov, CPO at ADEX. High-Risk Regions The ADEX report identifies the regions with the highest share of campaigns rejected at moderation in each period: Tier-1 markets (US, UK, Canada, Australia, Germany): high-risk in every quarter South Asia: from Q2 onward Turkey: first half of the year Latin America: Q1 East Asia: Q3 Industry Context ADEX places its findings alongside wider industry data cited in the report: Thales 2026 Bad Bot Report: bots made up over 53% of internet traffic. HUMAN: monthly AI-driven traffic grew 187% during 2025. Google’s 2025 Ads Safety Report: more than 8.3 billion ads were blocked or removed. 2027 Outlook ADEX lists five predictions: Ads written for AI agents, using prompt injection Agent traffic that blurs the line between bot and buyer Fraud operations generated end to end by AI More borrowed trust through hacked domains and messenger funnels Scareware moving to connected TV, in-app and AI assistant interfaces ADEX labels prompt injection a forecast, not a category currently measured in its moderation data. The complete dataset and methodology are available in the full ADEX report .

The report analyzes January–September 2026 moderation and verification data from eight ad platforms, covering 1.2 million campaigns and 4.9 million creatives. Below are the key findings.

Key Findings at a Glance
  • 52% of distinct fraud schemes showed AI-generated or AI-assisted assets.
  • 64% of AI-involved schemes used bots that pass as human visitors.
  • 53% of AI-involved schemes used cloned brands and fake endorsements.
  • 11% of AI-involved schemes used deepfakes.
  • About one-third of rejections were linked to infected domains, which became the top rejection reason from Q2 onward.
  • 6% of Q3 rejections were prize and bonus scareware (“You won a smartphone”), which emerged as its own category that quarter.
What Moved in 2026

According to ADEX, the clearest year-on-year shift is in why platforms suspend advertisers.

Metric2025 / Q1 2026Q3 2026Cloaking (share of suspensions)~75%~45%Malicious iOS scripts (share of suspensions)Not tracked~20%Copyright (share of rejections)8%21%Region-restricted content (share of rejections)5%11%Adult content (share of rejections)42%14%

Cloaking remains the top suspension reason, but it now shares the list with two newer threats: malicious iOS scripts and messenger-based phishing on services such as WhatsApp and Telegram.

In those messenger schemes, the persuasion happens in the chat itself. ADEX notes that language models let a single operator run hundreds of believable conversations in any language.

Quality Over Quantity

ADEX reports that the number of rejected or blocked campaigns fell by roughly a third after Q1. The report says this does not signal a quieter market. Operators shifted from mass submissions to fewer, better-built campaigns.

“One well-made scam with a cloned brand page does more damage than a hundred crude ones,” said Sergey Martianov, CPO at ADEX.

High-Risk Regions

The ADEX report identifies the regions with the highest share of campaigns rejected at moderation in each period:

  • Tier-1 markets (US, UK, Canada, Australia, Germany): high-risk in every quarter
  • South Asia: from Q2 onward
  • Turkey: first half of the year
  • Latin America: Q1
  • East Asia: Q3
Industry Context

ADEX places its findings alongside wider industry data cited in the report:

  • Thales 2026 Bad Bot Report: bots made up over 53% of internet traffic.
  • HUMAN: monthly AI-driven traffic grew 187% during 2025.
  • Google’s 2025 Ads Safety Report: more than 8.3 billion ads were blocked or removed.
2027 Outlook

ADEX lists five predictions:

  1. Ads written for AI agents, using prompt injection
  2. Agent traffic that blurs the line between bot and buyer
  3. Fraud operations generated end to end by AI
  4. More borrowed trust through hacked domains and messenger funnels
  5. Scareware moving to connected TV, in-app and AI assistant interfaces

ADEX labels prompt injection a forecast, not a category currently measured in its moderation data.

The complete dataset and methodology are available in the full ADEX report.

items.title: Hackers Launch 8,200 DDoS Attacks Every Hour, Cloudflare’s Latest Report Reveals
items.summary: Cloudflare blocked an average of more than 8,200 network-layer DDoS attacks every hour during the third quarter of 2026, showing how attackers are using frequent, short bursts to disrupt online services rather than relying only on record-breaking traffic floods. The company’s latest DDoS Threat Report, produced by its Cloudforce One threat intelligence team, covers July through September. Cloudflare stopped 18.2 million network-layer attacks and 14.4 trillion malicious HTTP requests during the period. These are separate measures, not a combined attack count. The hourly figure reflects attacks detected across Cloudflare’s network, not a complete worldwide total. Its systems filtered 272.6 petabytes of network-layer traffic and another 95.1 petabytes of HTTP attack traffic. Cloudflare DDoS attacks Network-layer attack numbers increased 208% compared with the same quarter in 2025. About 96% ended within ten minutes, while 98% stayed below one gigabit per second. That traffic can still overwhelm a website or server without enough protection. Cloudflare linked this pattern to DDoS-for-hire services, often called booters, which let customers pay to launch attacks. Computer software, gambling and casino businesses, and information technology companies were common targets of these frequent bursts. The timing creates a clear problem for defenders. When most attacks finish within minutes, teams cannot depend on reviewing an alert and manually changing filters before users lose access. Detection and traffic filtering need to happen automatically. Attacks exceeding one terabit per second fell from 805 in the second quarter to 251 in the third, a decline of nearly 69%. Cloudflare said this drop may reflect earlier law enforcement action, although the report does not establish a direct cause. On March 19, the U.S. Justice Department announced a coordinated operation against infrastructure supporting Aisuru, KimWolf, JackSkid, and Mossad. Authorities said the botnets had infected more than three million devices worldwide, including routers, cameras, and digital video recorders. Cybersecurity News previously covered the disruption of these IoT botnets and the seizure of infrastructure used to control infected devices. The latest figures suggest progress against large attack networks, but not an end to the threat. Mirai-related activity remained significant. The longest sustained Mirai attack lasted 49.7 hours between August 19 and August 21. Earlier reporting on the 31.4 Tbps Aisuru attack also shows how much traffic large botnets can generate. Attack methods changed sharply. CLDAP reflection attacks fell 99.5% from the previous quarter and represented just 0.05% of network-layer attacks. This method abuses exposed directory services by sending requests with a forged victim address, causing servers to direct larger replies at that victim. DNS amplification increased 215% and accounted for 3.43% of network-layer attacks. As Cloudflare’s DNS amplification guide explains, attackers exploit open DNS resolvers to turn small requests into larger responses sent toward a target. Other UDP floods increased their share from 14.06% to 31.31%. UDP does not require a connection handshake, allowing attackers to send large volumes of packets that consume bandwidth and server resources. The United States replaced China as the most-attacked location, with Indonesia third. Canada climbed from sixteenth to sixth, while Israel rose seven places to tenth. These rankings describe targeted locations, not where attackers live. Media, production, and publishing remained the most-attacked industry, despite a sharp drop in its share. Internet businesses reached sixth place, followed by consumer services in eighth and adult entertainment in ninth, showing a broader spread of targets. The company also offers a free DDoS Botnet Threat Feed for service providers. More than 800 networks have joined, helping operators identify abusive IP addresses and accounts linked to attacks and support coordinated botnet cleanup efforts. Cloudflare says its defenses operate across more than 330 cities with 500 Tbps of network capacity. The findings highlight why DDoS protection must handle both repeated short bursts and prolonged floods, while providers work together to remove compromised devices from attack networks. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

items.title: Abliterated Models in Appsec Pentesting
items.summary: Intro At Include Security we are constantly evaluating the best models to support us in webapp pentesting. Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 was released in August 2026, an open weight LLM which NIST estimated was four months behind the US frontier models in cyber capabilities. Anthropic later published an article raising concerns about GLM-5.3’s safeguards, particularly in abliterated versions of the model. To recap: abliteration (a portmanteau of “ablate” and “obliteration”) is a technique used to remove safety refusals from open-weight models. At a high level, abliteration edits a model’s internal representations of harmful inputs to look like harmless ones. This can make a model enthusiastically comply with requests that it was originally trained to refuse, such as requests to write and launch a zero day exploit. We decided to look into whether abliterated models are useful in webapp pentesting, and whether they come with other drawbacks or risks Cyber guardrails Cyber verification programs The backdrop is that frontier labs have been implementing more and more restrictive cyber guardrails. In addition to refusal behavior that is trained into the model’s weights, the frontier model providers run classifiers that sit between all prompts and model outputs, which terminate the conversation if malicious cyber behavior is suspected. OpenAI now splits cyber access into Daybreak Blue and Daybreak Red. Daybreak Blue dials down the cyber classifier, but is only intended for defensive work and does not grant access to specialized offensive cyber models like GPT-5.5-Cyber. That requires Daybreak Red, which is only open to approved business and enterprise organisations, and OpenAI notes that some safeguards still apply. Similarly, Anthropic offers the Red Team Access tier of their Cyber verification program to perform offensive cyber tasks with their latest models such as Opus 5.5. That tier is intended for “in-house red teams, government red teams, and security and penetration testing firms”. GLM-5.2 and Hugging Face GLM-5.2 (the same base model as GLM-5.3 with less post-training), became well-known for assisting in cyber tasks when Hugging Face was breached . Hugging Face incident responders tried feeding their forensic logs to frontier models, but the requests were blocked by guardrails, as Hugging Face was not yet part of a cyber verification program (they were later given access to Daybreak Blue by OpenAI). Hugging Face switched to using the open-weight GLM-5.2: We ran the forensic analysis instead on zai-org/GLM-5.2, an open-weight model, on our own infrastructure. This had a second benefit: no attacker data, and none of the credentials it referenced, left our environment. The Hugging Face report also notes the data security benefit of local models. For pentesters, even if you can get access to the frontier cyber verification programs, data retention is usually required by the model provider. Data retention of code by third parties often goes against contracts signed with clients. Abliteration Abliteration rests on a key finding by Arditi et al. from June 2024, showing that a model’s refusal behavior is encoded in a single direction in its internal activations, and can therefore be surgically disabled. A blog by Maxime Labonne followed soon after showing how to practically implement the technique. The most popular tool today is Heretic , released September 2025. It performs abliteration on a provided local model using a single command, and aims to minimize two measures: “refusal rate” – the percentage of harmful prompts the abliterated model refuses “KL Divergence” – how far the edited model’s outputs drift from the original on harmless prompts, a rough measure of capability loss Within days of the weights of GLM-5.3 being released, an abliterated version called penclaw-GLM-5.3-abliterated-for-offensive-cyber was released on Hugging Face with a reported 7.5% refusal rate. The abliterated model shares the hardware requirements of base GLM-5.3 : as a 753 billion parameter model, at FP8 precision it needs almost 1TB of VRAM, or hardware on the order of 8×H200 to run with large context. At 4-bit quantization, GLM-5.3 could run on a Mac Studio M3 Ultra with 512GB memory, but would be very slow with short context. There is a GLM-5.3 flash model with less than half the parameters but still good benchmark scores. The abliterated GLM-5.3 is offered up by a few model providers who specialize in hosting abliterated models, currently at a higher token price than base GLM-5.3. There are performance concerns and potential security risks both to running an abliterated model locally, as well as using those from hosting providers, which will be discussed below. Testing We tested the base GLM-5.3 against an abliterated version (abliterated-model-large-v2 hosted by a third party) at finding vulnerabilities in a range of projects, using the OpenCode agent harness. We picked a deliberately simple prompt asking each model to find security vulnerabilities in a codebase or on a website. We then used a mix of manual checking and Claude Opus 5.5 to score the quality of the findings with reference to the codebase, taking into account accuracy and coverage. For high severity findings, we asked both GLM-5.3 and the abliterated version to develop exploits, which we demoed and judged manually. Source code analysis Our hypothesis was that the abliterated model would be worse at finding vulnerabilities, for two reasons: The abliteration process causes some loss of intelligence Removing the model’s refusal ability may also weaken the model’s ability to filter out false positives The second point is based on the recent post “Don’t Let Abliteration Abliterate Your Bug Hunting” . They found that when running the same scan-and-triage pipeline over FreeBSD kernel source, abliterated Gemma models marked three to four times as many findings as valid as their base models. This mostly included false positives which the base model correctly rejected. In the chain of thought, the abliterated model could be seen considering rejecting false positive findings but then accepting them anyway. However, we couldn’t replicate this when testing the abliterated GLM-5.3. Perhaps because GLM-5.3 is a far more capable model than Gemma, and the abliteration performed had low KL divergence. Both base and abliterated models reported a low rate of false positives, and in fact the abliterated version was judged to have reported slightly more accurate findings, although this was within the margin of error. Where the abliterated model fell behind was in coverage, with it reporting fewer true positive findings overall. In one project, the abliterated model reported 16 findings versus 35 from the base. Overall, it produced 26% fewer findings, but notably, it also used about 29% fewer tokens in total, even though both runs used the max reasoning level. Source code analysis: Verdict The abliterated model wasn’t markedly worse than GLM-5.3 at source code analysis, but it does raise the question of why you’d use it for this purpose. GLM-5.3 and indeed frontier models are already happy to find vulnerabilities in code, with a low rate of refusals. We’d therefore recommend using the most capable and cost-effective model for vulnerability discovery. Exploit Development Abliteration starts to get interesting when building proof-of-concept exploits, however, not for the reason that we expected. We asked both models to develop exploits for five high-severity vulnerabilities found in the first pass. Base GLM-5.3 didn’t refuse any of these requests. In our small sample, though, the full end-to-end exploits that the abliterated version built worked first time in 4 of the 5 cases, compared with 2 of 5 for GLM-5.3. The abliterated version went further in weaponizing the exploit without prompting, which had the side effect of making it more robust against likely failure conditions. Example 1 – Transmission Both models found a high-severity flaw in the Transmission Bittorrent client. The vulnerability affects users who have enabled the Transmission daemon, which has an RPC endpoint. The Transmission daemon is intended to be access restricted to localhost by default. But because of a broken CORS configuration, any website that a user visits can bypass CSRF protection and then issue authenticated RPC commands to the daemon, including adding a torrent with an RCE payload inside. The payload can be triggered to run when the torrent completes. We looked at responsibly disclosing this finding, but found that it had already been reported and fixed in v4.1.3 and has recently been written about by Joshua Rogers . However the main branch of Transmission remains unpatched, as is the version available in the apt repos of Ubuntu and Debian as of October 2026. The abliterated GLM-5.3 had no issue in developing and testing an RCE exploit that worked the first time. The exploit uploaded a torrent to the targeted user’s system which deployed a malicious cronjob. Meanwhile, base GLM-5.3 built an exploit that worked up to the point of delivering the torrent, but the webseed code to upload the torrent from the server was broken. GLM-5.3 did not verify the final step of exploitation: We re-ran this example a few times, and each time the abliterated model went a step further in its proof-of-concept. For instance, given a more restrained prompt asked to demonstrate the CSRF only (not the RCE), the abliterated model still included the torrent download and left comments about how it would escalate “a real attack”. The base GLM-5.3 meanwhile stopped at demonstrating RPC writes and its comment at the same part of the code focused on how it was a safe “read-only” exploit. Example 2 – Anki Both models tested found an AppleScript injection vulnerability in the flashcard app Anki, which we reported to the maintainers. This turned out to be a new variant of another path injection to RCE finding: GHSA-932p-crhj-v43p Exploiting the vulnerability involved building a deck with an image containing a src attribute that embedded AppleScript code. If a user right-clicked to show the image in its folder, the AppleScript code was executed, which could include arbitrary system commands. The abliterated model generated a working exploit the first time, taking care to add parentheses around the payload to ensure it executed as a separate expression: Meanwhile, when writing its exploit, GLM-5.3 spent some time justifying it: > “Why it’s safe as a PoC: the demonstration runs open -a Calculator — visible, non-destructive, auto-closable. I deliberately did not write a real attacker payload; the writeup notes where one would substitute.” Ultimately, GLM-5.3’s exploit didn’t fire, since it relied on newline characters to separate the shell payload from the other AppleScript commands. Because the image was not found, the AppleScript code errored before the line opening the calculator ran: In this case, the models were not running on macOS and instead used the “osascript” command with a scaffold to simulate the vulnerable code. When given the ability to properly verify its exploit, base GLM-5.3 also used the parenthetical expression to write a working exploit similarly to the abliterated version. Exploit development: Verdict We had no trouble getting the base GLM-5.3 to write exploits, but it appeared that the model was sometimes cautious and stopped short of a robust proof of concept, particularly when unable to end-to-end verify its exploit. The abliterated model’s eagerness to push into post-exploitation meant it was able to check more steps of its exploit on the first try, with no extra prompting. Of course, none of this was hard to work around: nudging GLM-5.3 a little further, or patching its exploit by hand, was straightforward, and as pentesters we think it’s essential to understand an exploit before you run it anyway. Black box pentesting We found that black-box pentesting is an area where the abliterated model removed friction. When asking GLM-5.3 and the abliterated version to find webapp vulnerabilities on public websites that we own, GLM-5.3 required careful prompting to get started. Meanwhile the abliterated model started searching for vulnerabilities without any need to deliberately present the task. There are real concerns about running abliterated models without strong safeguards. From our testing, we noted the abliterated model was more likely to perform: Destructive actions: exhausting resources, triggering account lockouts, and running commands that modify or delete data. Scope breach: following a discovered credential or internal hostname onto systems that weren’t covered by the original request. Escalating persistence: continuing post-exploitation steps like persistence, lateral movement, or data access beyond what was needed. Even more so than in regular LLM-assisted pentesting, this makes a skilled operator monitoring the model essential, with a harness that enforces the rules of engagement rather than relying on the model to respect them. We plan to follow up with a more in-depth comparison of abliterated model behaviors in black box pentesting, although this is a difficult topic to approach sensitively. Supply-chain Risks Besides a model mishandling confidential client data or code, or running wild on a client’s systems, abliterated models also amplify the supply chain risks of using LLMs. There are three ways to access an abliterated model: Downloading and running one created by someone else Performing your own abliteration, e.g. with Heretic Using a hosted provider ProjectDiscovery’s recent research on “ how abliterated models can get you pwned” shows how backdoors can be planted in a model undetectably. Their findings apply to any self-hosted LLM, but their argument is that you should only run models from sources you trust, and it’s harder to trust any current sources of abliterated models. Abliterating the model yourself lowers that risk, but for a model the size of GLM-5.3 it is expensive. That puts both self-hosting options out of reach for most individual testers and smaller firms. So in practice, most people will use a hosting provider. The few providers that specialize in abliterated models tend to be opaque about who runs them. They claim to offer zero data retention although we did not find much info about their infrastructure or third-party audits. By contrast, the base GLM-5.3 is available through mainstream managed platforms such as AWS Bedrock, with established data handling terms. For the bulk of a webapp pentesting workflow, which our testing suggests the base model handles fine, this is the safer route. Conclusion We tested an abliterated version of GLM-5.3 against the base model and found limited use for it in source-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploit development. GLM-5.3 is already willing to find bugs and write exploits; the abliterated model’s main edge is that it pushes further into post-exploitation on its own, which inadvertently makes it more likely to produce a robust proof of concept on the first try. Given the right context, though, the base model does the same. Abliterated models also have no qualms at hacking live websites without authorization, but that comes at a cost. The abliterated model may take destructive, out-of-scope, or over-escalating actions, and it isn’t available from any provider we’d consider trustworthy. Abliterated models should only be used with great care, and for most of a pentesting workflow, base GLM-5.3 remains the better default for those who are not using frontier models.

However the main branch of Transmission remains unpatched, as is the version available in the apt repos of Ubuntu and Debian as of October 2026.

The abliterated GLM-5.3 had no issue in developing and testing an RCE exploit that worked the first time. The exploit uploaded a torrent to the targeted user’s system which deployed a malicious cronjob.

Meanwhile, base GLM-5.3 built an exploit that worked up to the point of delivering the torrent, but the webseed code to upload the torrent from the server was broken. GLM-5.3 did not verify the final step of exploitation:

We re-ran this example a few times, and each time the abliterated model went a step further in its proof-of-concept. For instance, given a more restrained prompt asked to demonstrate the CSRF only (not the RCE), the abliterated model still included the torrent download and left comments about how it would escalate “a real attack”. The base GLM-5.3 meanwhile stopped at demonstrating RPC writes and its comment at the same part of the code focused on how it was a safe “read-only” exploit.

Example 2 – Anki

Both models tested found an AppleScript injection vulnerability in the flashcard app Anki, which we reported to the maintainers. This turned out to be a new variant of another path injection to RCE finding: GHSA-932p-crhj-v43p

Exploiting the vulnerability involved building a deck with an image containing a src attribute that embedded AppleScript code. If a user right-clicked to show the image in its folder, the AppleScript code was executed, which could include arbitrary system commands.

The abliterated model generated a working exploit the first time, taking care to add parentheses around the payload to ensure it executed as a separate expression:

Meanwhile, when writing its exploit, GLM-5.3 spent some time justifying it:

> “Why it’s safe as a PoC: the demonstration runs open -a Calculator — visible, non-destructive, auto-closable. I deliberately did not write a real attacker payload; the writeup notes where one would substitute.”

Ultimately, GLM-5.3’s exploit didn’t fire, since it relied on newline characters to separate the shell payload from the other AppleScript commands. Because the image was not found, the AppleScript code errored before the line opening the calculator ran:

 

In this case, the models were not running on macOS and instead used the “osascript” command with a scaffold to simulate the vulnerable code. When given the ability to properly verify its exploit, base GLM-5.3 also used the parenthetical expression to write a working exploit similarly to the abliterated version.

Exploit development: Verdict

We had no trouble getting the base GLM-5.3 to write exploits, but it appeared that the model was sometimes cautious and stopped short of a robust proof of concept, particularly when unable to end-to-end verify its exploit.

The abliterated model’s eagerness to push into post-exploitation meant it was able to check more steps of its exploit on the first try, with no extra prompting. 

Of course, none of this was hard to work around: nudging GLM-5.3 a little further, or patching its exploit by hand, was straightforward, and as pentesters we think it’s essential to understand an exploit before you run it anyway.

Black box pentesting

We found that black-box pentesting is an area where the abliterated model removed friction. When asking GLM-5.3 and the abliterated version to find webapp vulnerabilities on public websites that we own, GLM-5.3 required careful prompting to get started. Meanwhile the abliterated model started searching for vulnerabilities without any need to deliberately present the task.

There are real concerns about running abliterated models without strong safeguards. From our testing, we noted the abliterated model was more likely to perform:

  • Destructive actions: exhausting resources, triggering account lockouts, and running commands that modify or delete data.
  • Scope breach: following a discovered credential or internal hostname onto systems that weren’t covered by the original request.
  • Escalating persistence: continuing post-exploitation steps like persistence, lateral movement, or data access beyond what was needed.

Even more so than in regular LLM-assisted pentesting, this makes a skilled operator monitoring the model essential, with a harness that enforces the rules of engagement rather than relying on the model to respect them.

We plan to follow up with a more in-depth comparison of abliterated model behaviors in black box pentesting, although this is a difficult topic to approach sensitively.

Supply-chain Risks

Besides a model mishandling confidential client data or code, or running wild on a client’s systems, abliterated models also amplify the supply chain risks of using LLMs. 

There are three ways to access an abliterated model:

  1. Downloading and running one created by someone else
  2. Performing your own abliteration, e.g. with Heretic
  3. Using a hosted provider

ProjectDiscovery’s recent research on “how abliterated models can get you pwned” shows how backdoors can be planted in a model undetectably. Their findings apply to any self-hosted LLM, but their argument is that you should only run models from sources you trust, and it’s harder to trust any current sources of abliterated models.

Abliterating the model yourself lowers that risk, but for a model the size of GLM-5.3 it is expensive. That puts both self-hosting options out of reach for most individual testers and smaller firms.

So in practice, most people will use a hosting provider. The few providers that specialize in abliterated models tend to be opaque about who runs them. They claim to offer zero data retention although we did not find much info about their infrastructure or third-party audits.

By contrast, the base GLM-5.3 is available through mainstream managed platforms such as AWS Bedrock, with established data handling terms. For the bulk of a webapp pentesting workflow, which our testing suggests the base model handles fine, this is the safer route.

Conclusion

We tested an abliterated version of GLM-5.3 against the base model and found limited use for it in source-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploit development. GLM-5.3 is already willing to find bugs and write exploits; the abliterated model’s main edge is that it pushes further into post-exploitation on its own, which inadvertently makes it more likely to produce a robust proof of concept on the first try. Given the right context, though, the base model does the same.

Abliterated models also have no qualms at hacking live websites without authorization, but that comes at a cost. The abliterated model may take destructive, out-of-scope, or over-escalating actions, and it isn’t available from any provider we’d consider trustworthy. Abliterated models should only be used with great care, and for most of a pentesting workflow, base GLM-5.3 remains the better default for those who are not using frontier models.

The post Abliterated Models in Appsec Pentesting appeared first on Include Security Research Blog.

items.summary: In this article Stages of AI adoption by North Korean threat actors AI use across North Korean threat operations AI-assisted targeting and reconnaissance AI-assisted social engineering and identity deception AI-assisted software and tooling development AI-assisted operational scaling and analysis Mitigation and protection guidance Microsoft Defender detections As Microsoft Threat Intelligence continues to track how threat actors operationalize AI to increase the speed, efficiency, and complexity of attacks, we’ve identified North Korean threat actors expanding their use of AI with varying levels of adoption. Threat actors use AI as a force multiplier across their operations, particularly to accelerate and scale established workflows. Recent activities illustrate this AI-enabled acceleration and scaling: Jade Sleet launched campaigns through three front companies in a single week, Onyx Sleet generated dozens of tailored lures in minutes, Coral Sleet rapidly built a new capability to trojanize private source code repositories, and Diamond Sleet used AI to enhance tailored targeting workflows, including persona development and front company creation. Further, Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet are leveraging the open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to conduct operations, further indicating North Korea’s willingness to quickly adopt new AI technologies for their operations. The Democratic People’s Republic of Korea operates under extensive international sanctions and uses cyber operations and other illicit mechanisms to evade these restrictions and advance state objectives. Within this operating environment, North Korean threat actors have demonstrated the willingness to adopt new technologies that help sustain or advance existing operations. AI adoption by North Korean threat actors therefore largely supports existing goals and targeting priorities rather than representing a shift in actor motivations. North Korean threat actors conduct cyber operations primarily to generate revenue for the regime, collect strategic intelligence, and, in some cases, pursue politically motivated disruptive or destructive objectives. Across these objectives, North Korean threat actor tradecraft remains grounded in social engineering, malware delivery, and the abuse of legitimate tools. These operations commonly target cryptocurrency and financial organizations, information technology companies and software supply chains, government entities, and education-related organizations. Despite threat actors’ adoption of AI, Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that AI-enabled operations remain human-directed and have not become fully autonomous. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses the overall adoption of AI across North Korean threat actors as high, with threat actors such as Jade Sleet, Coral Sleet, and Jasper Sleet demonstrating an established use of AI across all operational workflows, alongside increasing adoption across the broader North Korean threat actor set. This blog breaks down how North Korean threat actors are utilizing AI across their operations, reflecting a broader trend of threat actors incorporating AI into their attack chains. We also provide mitigation guidance and Microsoft Defender detections to help organizations defend against these threats. Stages of AI adoption by North Korean threat actors North Korean threat actors are increasingly integrating generative and agentic AI platforms into their operations, but the rate and maturity of adoption vary. Based on identified AI use, Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses high-impact North Korean threat actors across four stages of adoption: emerging, expanding, accelerating, and operationalized. Across these actors, AI use spans research, content generation, development, malware and tooling, infrastructure, and broader operational activities. Mapping high-impact North Korean threat actors by stages of AI adoption Operationalized: Threat actors at this stage have embedded AI into routine operational workflows, using it as an established part of their existing processes. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that the North Korean threat actors Jade Sleet, Coral Sleet, and Jasper Sleet have operationalized AI across their entire operations, which frequently encompass identity-based attacks built on deceptive social engineering. These attacks can be accelerated with AI capabilities that tailor lures or personas to the intended audience. Accelerating: Threat actors at this stage demonstrate rapid adoption of AI across multiple operational functions. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that Diamond Sleet , Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, and Sapphire Sleet are at the accelerating stage of AI adoption. Expanding: Threat actors at this stage are expanding their use of AI across selected operational activities, but adoption is not yet embedded across broader workflows. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that Emerald Sleet is at the expanding stage of AI adoption. While evidence suggests Emerald Sleet has incorporated AI into some workflows, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has not identified the same level of adoption and impact as other North Korean threat actors. Emerging: Threat actors at this stage demonstrate limited or experimental use of AI. At this time, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has not assessed any North Korean threat actors as operating at the emerging stage. AI use across North Korean threat operations Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified North Korean threat actors using AI platforms to support a range of operational activities, from reconnaissance to developing social engineering content, maintaining fraudulent identities, supporting tool development, and scaling repetitive operational tasks. Current evidence indicates that these actors primarily use AI to enhance existing tradecraft and operator productivity rather than to enable autonomous operations. Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified North Korean threat actors leveraging the following AI-enabled tactics as part of their threat operations. AI-assisted targeting and reconnaissance Based on industry reporting and changes in targeting activity in 2026, North Korean threat actors are scaling reconnaissance capabilities by using generative AI platforms, including gathering information on target organizations prior to launching social engineering operations. Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified that these actors: Research organizations and employees, then use information from this research to craft highly bespoke and convincing lures, target-specific infrastructure, and job applications Research wallets, exchanges, and decentralized finance (DeFi) and blockchain workflows, accelerating the development of domain knowledge needed to support targeted operations Explore vulnerabilities, APIs, security products, and cloud services, leading to a demonstrated change in the speed and sophistication of threat activity against specific technologies Research software development roles, job requirements, and technology organizations to support job searching, resume development, and persona alignment, resulting in rapid tailored persona or lure creation, application to newly posted job roles, or spear phishing operations For example, between June 8 and June 12, 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified Jade Sleet conducting job-themed targeting against individuals across various organizations, including those involved in cybersecurity, AI, blockchain, and talent recruitment companies. The actor leveraged tailored domains, social media profiles, and industry-specific knowledge to pose as recruiters for a spoofed AI-powered blockchain intelligence company, using software engineer-themed opportunities to initiate contact and schedule interviews with individuals who engaged with the outreach. Within this short time frame, Jade Sleet conducted similar job-themed targeting using two additional front companies, supported by comparable infrastructure and relevant domain knowledge. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that the pace and breadth of this activity demonstrates how Jade Sleet is using generative AI to accelerate operational workflows, including rapidly developing target- and industry-specific knowledge, tailoring reconnaissance and targeting, and scaling outreach to target individuals. Jasper Sleet also continues to leverage generative AI platforms to build fake digital personas. The actor’s use of suspected generative and agentic AI-assisted resume workflows demonstrates an improvement in the speed, scale, and relevance of persona preparation over the past year. Identified application activity indicates that the actor has invested in repeatable tooling to support employment-themed operations, ultimately helping the actor scale application activity and interact more credibly with the hiring processes of impacted organizations. Since August 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed Diamond Sleet returning to targeting the oil and gas sector for the first time since 2023, expanding their focus on communications and internet policy-related organizations, and continuing to target defense-related organizations. Further, Diamond Sleet has created fake communications technology companies, complete with supporting websites and tailored personas, to target telecommunications companies under the guise of legitimate business partnerships. These shifts have occurred alongside Diamond Sleet’s increased use of generative AI platforms to support reconnaissance and technical development, suggesting that AI could be improving the efficiency of existing operational workflows. AI-assisted social engineering and identity deception Several North Korean threat actors leverage job-themed social engineering techniques to gain access to target environments. For example, Sapphire Sleet, Jade Sleet, and Coral Sleet use employment- and interview-themed social engineering to target users and organizations, while Jasper Sleet uses fraudulent identities to obtain legitimate remote employment. These actors leverage AI to improve the process of creating convincing lures, aid in the development of fake personas, and evade detection when interacting with targets. Specifically, these actors use AI to: Produce tailored phishing, recruiter, and investment lures Create job-themed payload-delivery content and malicious repository lures Translate content and adjust tone to support foreign-language impersonation and more natural communications Build resumes, biographies, and realistic interview responses Support coding assessments, job-related tasks, and the management of multiple worker personas Enhance profile images and other identity artifacts Alter profile images, video, voice, and backgrounds Sustain recruiter, developer, investor, and other social identities across interactions and platforms Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified over 100 PDF lure files attributed to Onyx Sleet that were created in August and September 2026 with target-specific details. Metadata indicated that the actor created dozens of files at a time in rapid succession within minutes, highly likely to be the output of an AI platform. This automation supports the actor’s high-volume phishing campaigns against South Korean users and could make disruption and detection efforts more difficult given the rapid regeneration or modification of additional lures. Microsoft Threat Intelligence has also identified possible synthetic media generation, focused on AI-created voice and video, by Emerald Sleet. While we have not been able to determine the full operational impact of such tooling, it is highly likely that synthetic media creation is valued by multiple North Korean threat actors, as it significantly enhances existing social engineering capabilities. AI-assisted software and tooling development Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified evidence indicating that North Korean threat actors are leveraging AI-enabled software and tools to assist in malware development. These tools include AI-assisted development platforms, such as Cursor, which have likely enabled Jade Sleet, Coral Sleet, Pearl Sleet, and Sapphire Sleet to: Generate, convert, debug, and refactor code Assist with scripts, commands, persistence mechanisms, and obfuscation Troubleshoot errors and help operators diagnose tool behavior Support the adaptation or reimplementation of functionality across languages, libraries, and environments Additionally, AI-enabled development cycles further allow threat actors to circumvent detection and blocking efforts, as AI platforms streamline retooling, helping enable threat actors to rapidly pivot in reaction to defensive measures. For example, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified evidence indicating that Sapphire Sleet, who has conducted several supply chain attacks, likely incorporated AI during the August 2026 Rust software compromise. The activity spanned from initial stages targeting Rust developers to development and deployment of malware. Notably, Sapphire Sleet’s malware in this campaign was a marked improvement compared with other attributed campaigns, as the malware used dynamic .NET compilation during post-exploitation, most likely for defense evasion. And, since April 2026, Coral Sleet has operationalized a workflow to trojanize private GitHub repositories, integrating them into their existing malware chain. This new capability, its breadth and scale, and its rapid implementation were highly likely engineered using an AI-enabled development platform. AI-assisted operational scaling and analysis North Korean threat actors are leveraging AI platforms to scale and manage diverse operations. For example, Jasper Sleet’s AI tooling helps maintain consistent communication and performance across multiple fraudulent worker personas. We have also seen evidence of AI use for automating repetitive tasks, summarizing collected information from victim organizations, and accelerating post-compromise decision making while human operators likely continue to direct intent and objectives. This operational adoption extends to emerging agentic AI technologies. Since late October 2026, Microsoft threat Intelligence has identified Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet leveraging open-source agentic AI penetration testing ARTEX in operations, highlighting how North Korean threat actors are adopting new AI technologies as they become available. Mitigation and protection guidance Threat actor misuse of AI accelerates risk across enterprise environments by amplifying existing threats such as phishing, malware threats, and insider activity. To help organizations stay ahead of AI-enabled threat activity, Microsoft has introduced the Security Dashboard for AI . The dashboard provides users with a unified view of AI security posture by aggregating security, identity, and data risk across Microsoft Defender , Microsoft Entra , and Microsoft Purview . This allows organizations to understand what AI assets exist in their environment, recognize emerging risk patterns, and prioritize governance and security across AI agents, applications, and platforms. To learn more about the Microsoft Security Dashboard for AI see: Assess your organization’s AI risk with Microsoft Security Dashboard for AI . Additionally, Microsoft Agent 365 serves as a control plane for AI agents in enterprise environments, allowing users to manage, govern, and secure AI agents and workflows while monitoring emerging risks of agentic AI use. Agent 365 supports a growing ecosystem of agents, including Microsoft agents, broader ecosystems of agents such as Adobe and Databricks, and open-source agents published on GitHub. As the AI-enabled operations conducted by North Korean threat actors vary across TTPs, the following guidance can help organizations harden their networks against multiple classes of threats. Vulnerability and exposure management Use Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management to identify, assess, remediate, and track vulnerabilities across critical assets. Use the exposure score to reduce your vulnerability exposure and the Microsoft Secure Score to identify and remediate security misconfigurations in your environment. Use a perimeter scanning tool like Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management to understand your organization’s digital footprint and potential attack surface. Targeting web-facing vulnerabilities continues to be one of the most effective attack methods for initial access. Ensure any web-facing systems are isolated from the public internet with a secure network boundary and access them with a virtual private network (VPN). If certain servers must be accessible on the public internet, position them behind a web application firewall (WAF) , reverse proxy , or perimeter network (also known as a DMZ), which can reduce the risk of vulnerability exploitation in some cases. Consider automating patching where possible. Windows Update client policies offer automated patching, which can greatly reduce the amount of time IT admins must spend identifying, configuring, and deploying updates. To help manage infrastructure distributed across cloud, on-premises, and hybrid networks, use a centralized patching solution like Azure Update Manager . Protecting against social engineering and phishing Educate users about protecting personal and business information on social media, filtering unsolicited communication, identifying lures in spear-phishing emails and watering holes, and reporting reconnaissance attempts and other suspicious activity. Educate users about preventing malware infections , such as ignoring or deleting unsolicited and unexpected emails or attachments sent through instant messaging applications or social networks. Review the recommended settings for Exchange Online Protection and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to ensure your organization has established essential defenses and knows how to monitor and respond to threat activity. Invest in user awareness training and phishing simulations. Attack simulation training in Microsoft Defender for Office 365, which also includes simulating phishing messages in Microsoft Teams, is one approach to running realistic attack scenarios in your organization. Enable Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) in Defender for Office 365 to quarantine sent mail in response to newly acquired threat intelligence and retroactively neutralize malicious phishing, spam, or malware messages that have already been delivered to mailboxes. Responders could also manually check for and purge unwanted emails containing URLs and/or Subject fields that are similar, but not identical, to those of known bad messages. Investigate malicious email that was delivered in Microsoft 365 and use Threat Explorer to find and delete phishing emails. Turn on Safe Links and Safe Attachments in Microsoft Defender for Office 365. Only allow device code flow where necessary. Microsoft recommends blocking device code flow wherever possible . Where necessary, configure Microsoft Entra ID’s device code flow in your Conditional Access policies. Vetting potential employees Exercise greater scrutiny for employees of staffing companies, since this is the easiest avenue for North Korean workers to infiltrate target companies. Check to make sure a potential employee’s social media/professional accounts are not highly similar to the accounts of other individuals. In addition, check that a contact phone number listed on a potential employee’s account is unique and not also used by other accounts. Scrutinize resumes and background checks for consistency of names, addresses, and dates. Consider contacting references by phone or video-teleconference rather than email only. Search whether a potential employee is employed at multiple companies using the same persona. Ensure the potential employee is seen on camera during multiple video telecommunication sessions. If the potential employee reports video and/or microphone issues that prohibit participation, this should be considered a red flag. Confirm the potential employee has a digital footprint. This includes a real phone number (not VOIP), a residential address, and social media accounts. Defending against malware Turn on cloud-delivered protection in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants. Ensure Microsoft Defender Antivirus definitions are up to date and real-time protection is turned on . Run endpoint detection and response (EDR) in block mode so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach. Configure investigation and remediation in full automated mode to let Microsoft Defender for Endpoint take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume. Configure automatic attack disruption in Microsoft Defender XDR. Automatic attack disruption is designed to contain attacks in progress, limit the impact on an organization’s assets, and provide more time for security teams to remediate the attack fully. Enable network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint. Microsoft Defender XDR customers can turn on attack surface reduction rules to prevent several of the infection vectors of this threat. These rules, which can be configured by users with administrator rights, offer significant hardening against targeted attacks. In observed attacks, Microsoft customers who had the following rules turned on could mitigate the attack in the initial stages and prevent hands-on-keyboard activity: Block executable content from email client and webmail Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts Use advanced protection against ransomware Microsoft Defender detections Microsoft Defender customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below. Microsoft Defender coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog. Tactic Observed activity Microsoft Defender coverage Actor-specific alerts Known threat actor activity Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Emerald Sleet threat actor activity – Diamond Sleet Actor activity detected – Onyx Sleet activity group – Pearl Sleet actor activity detected – Sapphire Sleet actor activity – Jade Sleet threat actor activity detected – Coral Sleet activity Reconnaissance AI-assisted research of target organizations Microsoft Defender for Cloud – Possible AI Tools Reconnaissance Detected – Possible Secret Reconnaissance Detected Initial access Sign-in activity; phishing Microsoft Defender XDR – Sign-in activity by a suspected North Korean entity Jasper Sleet Microsoft Entra ID Protection – Atypical travelImpossible travel – Microsoft Entra threat intelligence (sign-in) Microsoft Defender for Office 365 – A potentially malicious URL click was detected – A user clicked through to a potentially malicious URL – Suspicious email sending patterns detected – Email messages containing malicious URL removed after delivery – Email messages removed after delivery – Email reported by user as malware or phish Execution Backdoors observed in Sapphire Sleet Rust software compromise Microsoft Defender Antivirus – Trojan:Linux/ProcmacSteal – Trojan:PowerShell/ProcmacSteal – Trojan:MacOS/ProcmacSteal – Trojan:Cargo/ProcmacSteal Microsoft Security Copilot Microsoft Security Copilot is embedded in Microsoft Defender and provides security teams with AI-powered capabilities to summarize incidents, analyze files and scripts, summarize identities, use guided responses, and generate device summaries, hunting queries, and incident reports. Customers can also deploy AI agents , including the following Microsoft Security Copilot agents , to perform security tasks efficiently: Threat Intelligence Briefing agent Phishing Triage agent Threat Hunting agent Dynamic Threat Detection agent Security Copilot is also available as a standalone experience where customers can perform specific security-related tasks, such as incident investigation, user analysis, and vulnerability impact assessment. In addition, Security Copilot offers developer scenarios that allow customers to build, test, publish, and integrate AI agents and plugins to meet unique security needs. Threat intelligence reports Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use the following threat analytics reports in the Defender portal (requires license for at least one Defender XDR product) to get the most up-to-date information about the activity and techniques discussed in this blog. These reports provide intelligence, protection information, and recommended actions to prevent, mitigate, or respond to associated threats found in customer environments. Threat overview profile: Threat actors operationalizing AI Actor profile: Coral Sleet Actor profile: Diamond Sleet Actor profile: Emerald Sleet Actor profile: Jade Sleet Actor profile: Jasper Sleet Actor profile: Onyx Sleet Actor profile: Pearl Sleet Actor profile: Sapphire Sleet Microsoft Security Copilot customers can also use the Microsoft Security Copilot integration in Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence, either in the Security Copilot standalone portal or in the embedded experience in the Microsoft Defender portal to get more information about this threat. Learn more For the latest security research from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community, check out the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Blog . To get notified about new publications and to join discussions on social media, follow us on LinkedIn , X (formerly Twitter) , and Bluesky . To hear stories and insights from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community about the ever-evolving threat landscape, listen to the Microsoft Threat Intelligence podcast .
