Within this short time frame, Jade Sleet conducted similar job-themed targeting using two additional front companies, supported by comparable infrastructure and relevant domain knowledge. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that the pace and breadth of this activity demonstrates how Jade Sleet is using generative AI to accelerate operational workflows, including rapidly developing target- and industry-specific knowledge, tailoring reconnaissance and targeting, and scaling outreach to target individuals.

Jasper Sleet also continues to leverage generative AI platforms to build fake digital personas. The actor’s use of suspected generative and agentic AI-assisted resume workflows demonstrates an improvement in the speed, scale, and relevance of persona preparation over the past year. Identified application activity indicates that the actor has invested in repeatable tooling to support employment-themed operations, ultimately helping the actor scale application activity and interact more credibly with the hiring processes of impacted organizations.

Since August 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed Diamond Sleet returning to targeting the oil and gas sector for the first time since 2023, expanding their focus on communications and internet policy-related organizations, and continuing to target defense-related organizations. Further, Diamond Sleet has created fake communications technology companies, complete with supporting websites and tailored personas, to target telecommunications companies under the guise of legitimate business partnerships. These shifts have occurred alongside Diamond Sleet’s increased use of generative AI platforms to support reconnaissance and technical development, suggesting that AI could be improving the efficiency of existing operational workflows.

AI-assisted social engineering and identity deception

Several North Korean threat actors leverage job-themed social engineering techniques to gain access to target environments. For example, Sapphire Sleet, Jade Sleet, and Coral Sleet use employment- and interview-themed social engineering to target users and organizations, while Jasper Sleet uses fraudulent identities to obtain legitimate remote employment. These actors leverage AI to improve the process of creating convincing lures, aid in the development of fake personas, and evade detection when interacting with targets. Specifically, these actors use AI to:

  • Produce tailored phishing, recruiter, and investment lures
  • Create job-themed payload-delivery content and malicious repository lures
  • Translate content and adjust tone to support foreign-language impersonation and more natural communications
  • Build resumes, biographies, and realistic interview responses
  • Support coding assessments, job-related tasks, and the management of multiple worker personas
  • Enhance profile images and other identity artifacts
  • Alter profile images, video, voice, and backgrounds
  • Sustain recruiter, developer, investor, and other social identities across interactions and platforms

Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified over 100 PDF lure files attributed to Onyx Sleet that were created in August and September 2026 with target-specific details. Metadata indicated that the actor created dozens of files at a time in rapid succession within minutes, highly likely to be the output of an AI platform. This automation supports the actor’s high-volume phishing campaigns against South Korean users and could make disruption and detection efforts more difficult given the rapid regeneration or modification of additional lures.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence has also identified possible synthetic media generation, focused on AI-created voice and video, by Emerald Sleet. While we have not been able to determine the full operational impact of such tooling, it is highly likely that synthetic media creation is valued by multiple North Korean threat actors, as it significantly enhances existing social engineering capabilities.

AI-assisted software and tooling development

Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified evidence indicating that North Korean threat actors are leveraging AI-enabled software and tools to assist in malware development. These tools include AI-assisted development platforms, such as Cursor, which have likely enabled Jade Sleet, Coral Sleet, Pearl Sleet, and Sapphire Sleet to:

  • Generate, convert, debug, and refactor code
  • Assist with scripts, commands, persistence mechanisms, and obfuscation
  • Troubleshoot errors and help operators diagnose tool behavior
  • Support the adaptation or reimplementation of functionality across languages, libraries, and environments

Additionally, AI-enabled development cycles further allow threat actors to circumvent detection and blocking efforts, as AI platforms streamline retooling, helping enable threat actors to rapidly pivot in reaction to defensive measures.

For example, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified evidence indicating that Sapphire Sleet, who has conducted several supply chain attacks, likely incorporated AI during the August 2026 Rust software compromise. The activity spanned from initial stages targeting Rust developers to development and deployment of malware. Notably, Sapphire Sleet’s malware in this campaign was a marked improvement compared with other attributed campaigns, as the malware used dynamic .NET compilation during post-exploitation, most likely for defense evasion.

And, since April 2026, Coral Sleet has operationalized a workflow to trojanize private GitHub repositories, integrating them into their existing malware chain. This new capability, its breadth and scale, and its rapid implementation were highly likely engineered using an AI-enabled development platform.

AI-assisted operational scaling and analysis

North Korean threat actors are leveraging AI platforms to scale and manage diverse operations. For example, Jasper Sleet’s AI tooling helps maintain consistent communication and performance across multiple fraudulent worker personas. We have also seen evidence of AI use for automating repetitive tasks, summarizing collected information from victim organizations, and accelerating post-compromise decision making while human operators likely continue to direct intent and objectives. This operational adoption extends to emerging agentic AI technologies. Since late October 2026, Microsoft threat Intelligence has identified Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet leveraging open-source agentic AI penetration testing ARTEX in operations, highlighting how North Korean threat actors are adopting new AI technologies as they become available.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Threat actor misuse of AI accelerates risk across enterprise environments by amplifying existing threats such as phishing, malware threats, and insider activity. To help organizations stay ahead of AI-enabled threat activity, Microsoft has introduced the Security Dashboard for AI. The dashboard provides users with a unified view of AI security posture by aggregating security, identity, and data risk across Microsoft Defender, Microsoft Entra, and Microsoft Purview. This allows organizations to understand what AI assets exist in their environment, recognize emerging risk patterns, and prioritize governance and security across AI agents, applications, and platforms. To learn more about the Microsoft Security Dashboard for AI see: Assess your organization’s AI risk with Microsoft Security Dashboard for AI.

Additionally, Microsoft Agent 365 serves as a control plane for AI agents in enterprise environments, allowing users to manage, govern, and secure AI agents and workflows while monitoring emerging risks of agentic AI use. Agent 365 supports a growing ecosystem of agents, including Microsoft agents, broader ecosystems of agents such as Adobe and Databricks, and open-source agents published on GitHub.

As the AI-enabled operations conducted by North Korean threat actors vary across TTPs, the following guidance can help organizations harden their networks against multiple classes of threats.

Vulnerability and exposure management

  • Use Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management to identify, assess, remediate, and track vulnerabilities across critical assets. Use the exposure score to reduce your vulnerability exposure and the Microsoft Secure Score to identify and remediate security misconfigurations in your environment.
  • Use a perimeter scanning tool like Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management to understand your organization’s digital footprint and potential attack surface. Targeting web-facing vulnerabilities continues to be one of the most effective attack methods for initial access.
  • Ensure any web-facing systems are isolated from the public internet with a secure network boundary and access them with a virtual private network (VPN). If certain servers must be accessible on the public internet, position them behind a web application firewall (WAF), reverse proxy, or perimeter network (also known as a DMZ), which can reduce the risk of vulnerability exploitation in some cases.
  • Consider automating patching where possible. Windows Update client policies offer automated patching, which can greatly reduce the amount of time IT admins must spend identifying, configuring, and deploying updates.
  • To help manage infrastructure distributed across cloud, on-premises, and hybrid networks, use a centralized patching solution like Azure Update Manager.

Protecting against social engineering and phishing

  • Educate users about protecting personal and business information on social media, filtering unsolicited communication, identifying lures in spear-phishing emails and watering holes, and reporting reconnaissance attempts and other suspicious activity.
  • Educate users about preventing malware infections, such as ignoring or deleting unsolicited and unexpected emails or attachments sent through instant messaging applications or social networks.
  • Review the recommended settings for Exchange Online Protection and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to ensure your organization has established essential defenses and knows how to monitor and respond to threat activity.
  • Invest in user awareness training and phishing simulations. Attack simulation training in Microsoft Defender for Office 365, which also includes simulating phishing messages in Microsoft Teams, is one approach to running realistic attack scenarios in your organization.
  • Enable Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) in Defender for Office 365 to quarantine sent mail in response to newly acquired threat intelligence and retroactively neutralize malicious phishing, spam, or malware messages that have already been delivered to mailboxes.
  • Responders could also manually check for and purge unwanted emails containing URLs and/or Subject fields that are similar, but not identical, to those of known bad messages.
  • Investigate malicious email that was delivered in Microsoft 365 and use Threat Explorer to find and delete phishing emails.
  • Turn on Safe Links and Safe Attachments in Microsoft Defender for Office 365.
  • Only allow device code flow where necessary. Microsoft recommends blocking device code flow wherever possible. Where necessary, configure Microsoft Entra ID’s device code flow in your Conditional Access policies.

Vetting potential employees

  • Exercise greater scrutiny for employees of staffing companies, since this is the easiest avenue for North Korean workers to infiltrate target companies.
  • Check to make sure a potential employee’s social media/professional accounts are not highly similar to the accounts of other individuals. In addition, check that a contact phone number listed on a potential employee’s account is unique and not also used by other accounts.
  • Scrutinize resumes and background checks for consistency of names, addresses, and dates. Consider contacting references by phone or video-teleconference rather than email only.
  • Search whether a potential employee is employed at multiple companies using the same persona.
  • Ensure the potential employee is seen on camera during multiple video telecommunication sessions. If the potential employee reports video and/or microphone issues that prohibit participation, this should be considered a red flag.
  • Confirm the potential employee has a digital footprint. This includes a real phone number (not VOIP), a residential address, and social media accounts.

Defending against malware

  • Turn on cloud-delivered protection in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
  • Ensure Microsoft Defender Antivirus definitions are up to date and real-time protection is turned on.
  • Run endpoint detection and response (EDR) in block mode so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
  • Configure investigation and remediation in full automated mode to let Microsoft Defender for Endpoint take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
  • Configure automatic attack disruption in Microsoft Defender XDR. Automatic attack disruption is designed to contain attacks in progress, limit the impact on an organization’s assets, and provide more time for security teams to remediate the attack fully.
  • Enable network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
  • Microsoft Defender XDR customers can turn on attack surface reduction rules to prevent several of the infection vectors of this threat. These rules, which can be configured by users with administrator rights, offer significant hardening against targeted attacks. In observed attacks, Microsoft customers who had the following rules turned on could mitigate the attack in the initial stages and prevent hands-on-keyboard activity:
    • Block executable content from email client and webmail
    • Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion
    • Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts
    • Use advanced protection against ransomware
Microsoft Defender detections

Microsoft Defender customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below. Microsoft Defender coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog.

Microsoft Security Copilot is embedded in Microsoft Defender and provides security teams with AI-powered capabilities to summarize incidents, analyze files and scripts, summarize identities, use guided responses, and generate device summaries, hunting queries, and incident reports.

Customers can also deploy AI agents, including the following Microsoft Security Copilot agents, to perform security tasks efficiently:

  • Threat Intelligence Briefing agent

  • Threat Hunting agent
  • Dynamic Threat Detection agent

Security Copilot is also available as a standalone experience where customers can perform specific security-related tasks, such as incident investigation, user analysis, and vulnerability impact assessment. In addition, Security Copilot offers developer scenarios that allow customers to build, test, publish, and integrate AI agents and plugins to meet unique security needs.

Threat intelligence reports

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use the following threat analytics reports in the Defender portal (requires license for at least one Defender XDR product) to get the most up-to-date information about the activity and techniques discussed in this blog. These reports provide intelligence, protection information, and recommended actions to prevent, mitigate, or respond to associated threats found in customer environments.

items.title: IDC MarketScape names Microsoft a Leader in the 2026 Worldwide Modern Endpoint Security for Enterprises Vendor Assessment
items.summary: Today, we’re proud to share thatMicrosoft has been named a Leader in the 2026 IDC MarketScape for Worldwide Modern Endpoint Security for Enterprises (Doc #US54123526, September 2026). The IDC Marketscape calls out three strengths that we believe matter most in endpoint security today: Autonomous attack disruption and predictive shielding contain ransomware and identity attacks in minutes, at a meaningful scale. Agentic AI through Security Copilot is now generally available, with measured gains in alert accuracy and analyst time saved. The company offers broad native cross-platform coverage plus sovereign cloud and data residency options for regulated and multinational customers. Read the IDC report IDC MarketScape vendor analysis model is designed to provide an overview of the competitive fitness of technology and suppliers in a given market. The research methodology utilizes a rigorous scoring methodology based on both qualitative and quantitative criteria that results in a single graphical illustration of each supplier’s position within a given market. The Capabilities score measures supplier product, go-to-market and business execution in the short-term. The Strategy score measures alignment of supplier strategies with customer requirements in a 3-5-year timeframe. Supplier market share is represented by the size of the icons. The most critical moment in any attack is when it moves from access to action. That’s when ransomware detonates, stolen credentials are put to work, and, increasingly, a manipulated AI agent turns a user’s own data and tools against them. And threat actors are now using teams of AI agents to execute attacks faster and more relentlessly. Between 2025 and 2026, Microsoft Security researchers observed a more than 15% increase in ransomware detonations against enterprises. 1 When an attacker can move from first foothold to encryption in minutes, protection on the endpoint must act at the same speed, without waiting for a person to connect the dots. Protection that acts while the attack is still unfolding The IDC MarketScape highlights that “Automatic attack disruption contains compromised devices, users, and IP addresses in near real time, and predictive shielding proactively hardens likely next attacker moves.” Built into Microsoft Defender , attack disruption uses AI and signals from the endpoint and across identities, email, and cloud to recognize multistage attacks, such as ransomware, as they happen. It then automatically contains the affected devices and users to stop the attacker from moving laterally. Against attacks that move in minutes, protection has to work autonomously, while the attack is still in progress and before it can spread. QNET, a global direct-selling company, saw this firsthand. Defender identified an active ransomware attack, isolated the compromised device, and stopped the second-stage payload within 128 seconds of the first high-severity alert . A foundation built for agentic security Stopping an attack like QNET’s in seconds starts with the right foundation. Attack disruption succeeds because Defender can see activity across endpoints, identities, email, and cloud, understand what that activity means, and act on it natively. The IDC MarketScape highlights that “the Defender portal unifies incident and alert queues, graph-based incident views, and advanced hunting, correlating signals from endpoint, identity, email, SaaS, and cloud sources into a single incident.” That foundation depends on three layers working as one. Signals and sensors give the system awareness across the entire environment. Context turns those signals into understanding: what is happening, what is exposed, how an attacker could move, and what matters most. Actuators, like attack disruption, turn that understanding into protective action. To protect against the latest AI-based threats, these layers need to work in unison. That’s why, on September 23, 2026, we announced the integrated security operations center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender . ISOC brings security information and event management (SIEM) and Defender’s threat protection together, giving people and agents shared signals, shared context, and shared controls to see, understand, and act across the environment as one. On top of that foundation, we continue to strengthen what Defender can see: Richer endpoint signals: Defender provides more than 200 native event types for threat hunting. Custom data collection extends that visibility by letting security teams collect specialized telemetry to support tailored detections and advanced hunting. Comprehensive signals across your environment: Microsoft Sentinel now provides more than 500 connectors to ingest security-relevant data from across your organization’s digital estate. This breadth gives defenders the context to connect activity across otherwise fragmented systems, detect threats that no single signal would reveal, and investigate and respond with greater confidence. Agentic AI built into the flow of work With signals, context, and actuators working as one in Microsoft Defender, agents have what they need to be effective: the visibility to see what’s happening, the context to understand it, and the controls to act on it. IDC notes that AI is deeply embedded across the Defender platform, with agentic AI now generally available and delivering “measured gains in alert accuracy and analyst time saved.” One platform to see, understand, and protect local AI agents The same visibility, context, and controls that make agents effective for defenders also make it possible to secure the agents employees use every day. Developers and knowledge workers now run local agents, from coding assistants to agentic development environments, with access to data, credentials, tools, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. IDC advises buyers to ask how vendors secure AI on the endpoint, including visibility into local models and agent activity. With Defender, security teams can see those agents, understand their reach, and protect them as they operate. See every local agent: Discovery of local agents and their configured MCP servers is available on Windows and macOS, covering more than 50 supported agents and MCP servers, including claw-based agents such as OpenClaw. Understand their reach: The exposure graph in Defender maps each agent’s blast radius across devices, identities, and MCP connections, and teams can investigate agent activity in advanced hunting alongside data from endpoints, identities, email, and cloud. Protect agents as they operate: Runtime protection, in preview on Windows, stops malicious instructions, such as prompt injection hidden in a file or web page, before an agent acts on them, and raises an alert with agent and session context. In a threat landscape being reshaped by AI, Microsoft Defender will continue to deliver leading endpoint security for any platform with a focus on reducing exposure, disrupting active attacks in your environment, and strengthening resilience across the entire organization. To see where security operations are headed next, join Rob Lefferts at Microsoft Ignite for the session: The Alert Is Dead. The Blueprint for the Agentic SOC. Today, we’re proud to share thatMicrosoft has been named a Leader in the 2026 IDC MarketScape for Worldwide Modern Endpoint Security for Enterprises (Doc #US54123526, September 2026). The IDC Marketscape calls out three strengths that we believe matter most in endpoint security today:

  • Autonomous attack disruption and predictive shielding contain ransomware and identity attacks in minutes, at a meaningful scale.
  • Agentic AI through Security Copilot is now generally available, with measured gains in alert accuracy and analyst time saved.
  • The company offers broad native cross-platform coverage plus sovereign cloud and data residency options for regulated and multinational customers.
Read the IDC report

IDC MarketScape vendor analysis model is designed to provide an overview of the competitive fitness of technology and suppliers in a given market. The research methodology utilizes a rigorous scoring methodology based on both qualitative and quantitative criteria that results in a single graphical illustration of each supplier’s position within a given market. The Capabilities score measures supplier product, go-to-market and business execution in the short-term. The Strategy score measures alignment of supplier strategies with customer requirements in a 3-5-year timeframe. Supplier market share is represented by the size of the icons.

The most critical moment in any attack is when it moves from access to action. That’s when ransomware detonates, stolen credentials are put to work, and, increasingly, a manipulated AI agent turns a user’s own data and tools against them. And threat actors are now using teams of AI agents to execute attacks faster and more relentlessly. Between 2025 and 2026, Microsoft Security researchers observed a more than 15% increase in ransomware detonations against enterprises.1 When an attacker can move from first foothold to encryption in minutes, protection on the endpoint must act at the same speed, without waiting for a person to connect the dots.

Protection that acts while the attack is still unfolding

The IDC MarketScape highlights that “Automatic attack disruption contains compromised devices, users, and IP addresses in near real time, and predictive shielding proactively hardens likely next attacker moves.” Built into Microsoft Defender, attack disruption uses AI and signals from the endpoint and across identities, email, and cloud to recognize multistage attacks, such as ransomware, as they happen. It then automatically contains the affected devices and users to stop the attacker from moving laterally. Against attacks that move in minutes, protection has to work autonomously, while the attack is still in progress and before it can spread.

QNET, a global direct-selling company, saw this firsthand. Defender identified an active ransomware attack, isolated the compromised device, and stopped the second-stage payload within 128 seconds of the first high-severity alert.

A foundation built for agentic security

Stopping an attack like QNET’s in seconds starts with the right foundation. Attack disruption succeeds because Defender can see activity across endpoints, identities, email, and cloud, understand what that activity means, and act on it natively. The IDC MarketScape highlights that “the Defender portal unifies incident and alert queues, graph-based incident views, and advanced hunting, correlating signals from endpoint, identity, email, SaaS, and cloud sources into a single incident.”

That foundation depends on three layers working as one. Signals and sensors give the system awareness across the entire environment. Context turns those signals into understanding: what is happening, what is exposed, how an attacker could move, and what matters most. Actuators, like attack disruption, turn that understanding into protective action. To protect against the latest AI-based threats, these layers need to work in unison.

That’s why, on September 23, 2026, we announced the integrated security operations center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender. ISOC brings security information and event management (SIEM) and Defender’s threat protection together, giving people and agents shared signals, shared context, and shared controls to see, understand, and act across the environment as one. On top of that foundation, we continue to strengthen what Defender can see:

  • Richer endpoint signals: Defender provides more than 200 native event types for threat hunting. Custom data collection extends that visibility by letting security teams collect specialized telemetry to support tailored detections and advanced hunting.
  • Comprehensive signals across your environment: Microsoft Sentinel now provides more than 500 connectors to ingest security-relevant data from across your organization’s digital estate. This breadth gives defenders the context to connect activity across otherwise fragmented systems, detect threats that no single signal would reveal, and investigate and respond with greater confidence.
Agentic AI built into the flow of work

With signals, context, and actuators working as one in Microsoft Defender, agents have what they need to be effective: the visibility to see what’s happening, the context to understand it, and the controls to act on it. IDC notes that AI is deeply embedded across the Defender platform, with agentic AI now generally available and delivering “measured gains in alert accuracy and analyst time saved.”

One platform to see, understand, and protect local AI agents

The same visibility, context, and controls that make agents effective for defenders also make it possible to secure the agents employees use every day. Developers and knowledge workers now run local agents, from coding assistants to agentic development environments, with access to data, credentials, tools, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. IDC advises buyers to ask how vendors secure AI on the endpoint, including visibility into local models and agent activity. With Defender, security teams can see those agents, understand their reach, and protect them as they operate.

  • See every local agent: Discovery of local agents and their configured MCP servers is available on Windows and macOS, covering more than 50 supported agents and MCP servers, including claw-based agents such as OpenClaw.
  • Understand their reach: The exposure graph in Defender maps each agent’s blast radius across devices, identities, and MCP connections, and teams can investigate agent activity in advanced hunting alongside data from endpoints, identities, email, and cloud.
  • Protect agents as they operate: Runtime protection, in preview on Windows, stops malicious instructions, such as prompt injection hidden in a file or web page, before an agent acts on them, and raises an alert with agent and session context.

In a threat landscape being reshaped by AI, Microsoft Defender will continue to deliver leading endpoint security for any platform with a focus on reducing exposure, disrupting active attacks in your environment, and strengthening resilience across the entire organization.

To see where security operations are headed next, join Rob Lefferts at Microsoft Ignite for the session: The Alert Is Dead. The Blueprint for the Agentic SOC.

Risks and Mitigation of Malware Explained: Top 5 Strategies
items.summary: Key Takeaways Malware can cause data theft, operational disruption, financial losses, reputational damage, and legal consequences. EDR solutions use behavioral analysis and machine learning to detect suspicious activity, isolate threats, and limit malware spread. Regular software updates and patches help close vulnerabilities that attackers exploit to deploy malware. Strong authentication, least-privilege access, and continuous employee security awareness training reduce the risk of malware infections. Reliable backups, incident response plans, network monitoring, and segmentation help contain attacks and restore affected systems. Malware—short for malicious software and malicious programs—is one of the most dangerous cybersecurity threats today. From computer viruses and spyware to ransomware and trojans, these harmful programs are designed to: Sneak into systems Steal sensitive data Shut down operations entirely Cybercriminals are constantly developing new and more advanced forms of malware. Every single day, over half a million new malware samples are discovered globally, showing just how fast these threats are evolving. For businesses, the consequences can be severe. A single malware attack can lead to: Massive data loss Costly downtime Long-lasting damage to a company’s reputation Recovering from an attack can take weeks or months and cost millions, depending on how severe and long it is. In this blog, we’ll explore how to mitigate malware, understand the risks it poses to organizations, and implement practical strategies to prevent infections and limit damage. Understanding Malware and Its Evolving Threat Malware comes in many forms: Type of Malware Description Ransomware Locks or encrypts files and demands payment to restore access. Spyware Secretly monitors user activity to steal information like passwords or payment data. Virus Attaches to files and spreads to other systems when the infected file is shared or opened. Worm Infected computers can become the breeding ground for worms, which replicate themselves and spread without needing user action. Trojan (or Trojan horse) Disguises itself as legitimate software or a computer program but contains harmful code. Adware Floods devices with pop-up ads and can introduce unwanted software or more serious threats. How Malware Has Changed Over Time Malware is not only more common now, but also more advanced. In the last decade, attacks have surged, and newer types are built to get past traditional security. Modern malware is much harder to detect and stop. For example: Polymorphic malware changes its code to avoid detection. Fileless malware hides in system memory, leaving no trace on hard drives. Social engineering tricks people into clicking links, downloading files, or giving access. Obfuscation methods disguise malicious code to look harmless, confusing both users and antivirus tools. How Malware Gets In Attackers don’t rely on just one method—they exploit multiple weak points to increase their chances of success. Here are the most common entryways: Source of Threat Description Phishing Emails Look real but contain links or attachments that lead to malicious websites. Compromised Websites Automatically download harmful software without your knowledge (drive-by downloads). Removable Media USB drives left in public or shared between devices can spread malware. Unverified Software Computer software from unofficial sources or peer-to-peer networks may carry malware. Outdated Software Contains security flaws that hackers can easily exploit, particularly on personal computers if they are not regularly updated. Discover Key Insights and Detection Methods to Protect against Malware Behavior analysis and machine learning Real-time & offline scanning capabilities In-depth detection rates and case study data Download the Whitepaper Now! Key Risks Malware Poses to Organizations Security risk of malware range from data theft and financial losses to operational disruption and regulatory penalties. Understanding malware risks is essential for protecting business operations, sensitive data, and organizational reputation. 1. Data Loss and Theft Malware, including mobile malware, can pose a serious risk to sensitive information. It can steal or compromise: Personal details Financial data Intellectual property Customer records Once malware gains access to a system, it can transmit stolen data to cybercriminals, leading to consequences such as: Identity theft Financial fraud Industrial espionage 2. Operational Disruption Malware can seriously disrupt business operations by providing remote access to cybercriminals. Ransomware , a kind of malware, can: Lock infected systems Encrypt important files, making them inaccessible Demand a ransom payment for file recovery Not paying the ransom can lead to: Delayed recovery Significant downtime Major disruption to services 3. Financial Damage Malware attacks can have a significant financial impact. Costs may include: Ransom payments (if applicable) System recovery and data restoration expenses Efforts to mitigate further damage Additional financial burdens come from: Lost productivity Operational downtime Customer dissatisfaction Altogether, these factors can severely affect a company’s bottom line. 4. items.summary_html:
Key Takeaways
  • Malware can cause data theft, operational disruption, financial losses, reputational damage, and legal consequences.
  • EDR solutions use behavioral analysis and machine learning to detect suspicious activity, isolate threats, and limit malware spread.
  • Regular software updates and patches help close vulnerabilities that attackers exploit to deploy malware.
  • Strong authentication, least-privilege access, and continuous employee security awareness training reduce the risk of malware infections.
  • Reliable backups, incident response plans, network monitoring, and segmentation help contain attacks and restore affected systems.

Malware—short for malicious software and malicious programs—is one of the most dangerous cybersecurity threats today. From computer viruses and spyware to ransomware and trojans, these harmful programs are designed to:  

  • Sneak into systems
  • Steal sensitive data
  • Shut down operations entirely 

Cybercriminals are constantly developing new and more advanced forms of malware. Every single day, over half a million new malware samples are discovered globally, showing just how fast these threats are evolving. 

For businesses, the consequences can be severe. A single malware attack can lead to:

  • Massive data loss
  • Costly downtime
  • Long-lasting damage to a company’s reputation 

Recovering from an attack can take weeks or months and cost millions, depending on how severe and long it is.

In this blog, we’ll explore how to mitigate malware, understand the risks it poses to organizations, and implement practical strategies to prevent infections and limit damage.

Understanding Malware and Its Evolving Threat

Malware comes in many forms:

Type of Malware Description RansomwareLocks or encrypts files and demands payment to restore access.Spyware Secretly monitors user activity to steal information like passwords or payment data.VirusAttaches to files and spreads to other systems when the infected file is shared or opened.WormInfected computers can become the breeding ground for worms, which replicate themselves and spread without needing user action.Trojan (or Trojan horse)Disguises itself as legitimate software or a computer program but contains harmful code.Adware Floods devices with pop-up ads and can introduce unwanted software or more serious threats.
How Malware Has Changed Over Time

Malware is not only more common now, but also more advanced. In the last decade, attacks have surged, and newer types are built to get past traditional security. 

Modern malware is much harder to detect and stop. For example:

  1. Polymorphic malware changes its code to avoid detection.
  2. Fileless malware hides in system memory, leaving no trace on hard drives.
  3. Social engineering tricks people into clicking links, downloading files, or giving access.
  4. Obfuscation methods disguise malicious code to look harmless, confusing both users and antivirus tools.
How Malware Gets In

Attackers don’t rely on just one method—they exploit multiple weak points to increase their chances of success. Here are the most common entryways:

Source of Threat Description Phishing EmailsLook real but contain links or attachments that lead to malicious websites. Compromised Websites Automatically download harmful software without your knowledge (drive-by downloads).Removable MediaUSB drives left in public or shared between devices can spread malware.Unverified SoftwareComputer software from unofficial sources or peer-to-peer networks may carry malware.Outdated SoftwareContains security flaws that hackers can easily exploit, particularly on personal computers if they are not regularly updated.
Discover Key Insights and Detection Methods to Protect against Malware
  • Behavior analysis and machine learning
  • Real-time & offline scanning capabilities
  • In-depth detection rates and case study data
Download the Whitepaper Now!
Key Risks Malware Poses to Organizations

Security risk of malware range from data theft and financial losses to operational disruption and regulatory penalties. Understanding malware risks is essential for protecting business operations, sensitive data, and organizational reputation.

1. Data Loss and Theft

Malware, including mobile malware, can pose a serious risk to sensitive information.

It can steal or compromise:

  • Personal details
  • Financial data
  • Intellectual property
  • Customer records

Once malware gains access to a system, it can transmit stolen data to cybercriminals, leading to consequences such as:

  • Identity theft
  • Financial fraud
  • Industrial espionage
2. Operational Disruption

Malware can seriously disrupt business operations by providing remote access to cybercriminals.

Ransomware, a kind of malware, can:

  • Lock infected systems
  • Encrypt important files, making them inaccessible
  • Demand a ransom payment for file recovery

Not paying the ransom can lead to:

  • Delayed recovery
  • Significant downtime
  • Major disruption to services
3. Financial Damage

Malware attacks can have a significant financial impact. Costs may include:

  • Ransom payments (if applicable)
  • System recovery and data restoration expenses
  • Efforts to mitigate further damage

Additional financial burdens come from:

  • Lost productivity
  • Operational downtime
  • Customer dissatisfaction

Altogether, these factors can severely affect a company’s bottom line.

4. Reputational Harm

A single malware attack can seriously hurt a company’s reputation. If sensitive data gets leaked and operations get destroyed, it can lead to the loss of trust and loyalty from:

  • Customers
  • Business partners
  • Regulators

Consequences of this loss of confidence may include:

  • Decline in customer loyalty
  • Harder to get new customers
  • More attention from regulators
5. Regulatory and Legal Consequences

Organizations must follow data protection laws. A malware attack can lead to serious legal trouble, such as:

  • Non-compliance fines
  • Lawsuits

Businesses may be held liable for failing to protect customer data. This can further harm the organization’s reputation and financial stability. The following malware mitigation strategies can help organizations reduce these risks and strengthen their defenses.

Top 5 Malware Mitigation Strategies

Different types of malware mitigation include endpoint detection and response, regular patching, strong access controls, employee security awareness training, and reliable backups. These strategies help organizations prevent infections, detect threats early, and limit the impact of malware attacks.

1. Strengthen Endpoint Detection and Response

Endpoint security solutions (EDR) are key for detecting and responding to malware in real time.

EDR solutions utilize advanced technologies like:

  • Behavioral analysis
  • Machine learning

Key capabilities include:

  • Detecting unusual activity across the network
  • Reanalyzing previously approved files and flagging malicious ones
  • Quickly isolating threats to prevent further spread

EDR also helps minimize the impact of threats and attacks on systems and data.

2. Regularly Update and Patch Systems

Regular updates are a key defense against malware. Old software often has weaknesses that hackers target.

Key areas to keep updated include:

  • Operating systems
  • Browsers
  • Plugins

Regular patching helps address known vulnerabilities promptly. Automating patch management helps in:

  • Reducing the risk of human error
  • Ensuring critical updates are not missed
3. Implement Strong Authentication and Access Controls

Enforcing strong authentication practices is crucial to preventing unauthorized access.

  • Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): Use MFA on all critical systems and accounts for added security beyond passwords.
  • Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP): Give users access only to what they need to lower security risks.
  • Conditional Access Policies: Require things like MFA or location limits before allowing access to sensitive systems.
4. Educate Employees Through Continuous Security Awareness Training

Malware often spreads due to human mistakes like phishing attacks and downloading malicious files.

Continuous security awareness training helps employees:

  • Stay informed about the latest threats
  • Recognize and avoid suspicious activity

Effective training strategies include:

  • Simulated phishing tests
  • Providing real-world threat examples
  • Promoting a culture of quick, blame-free reporting
5. Maintain Reliable, Tested Backups and an Incident Response Plan

Attacks can still occur despite strong preventive measures. Reliable and regularly tested backups are essential for data recovery.

The backup strategy should include:

  • Offline backups
  • Cloud backups

These backups ensure the quick restoration of lost or corrupted data.

An Incident Response Plan (IRP) should guide the team through:

  • Detection – Quickly identifying the attack to mitigate its impact
  • Containment – Isolating the threat to prevent further spread
  • Recovery – Restoring affected systems and data to normal operation

A structured incident response plan and detailed security telemetry can help reduce malware investigation time by enabling teams to identify suspicious activity, understand the attack’s impact, and prioritize containment actions.

Speed is critical during incident response because:

  • Regulatory bodies may require rapid data recovery to meet legal and industry standards.
  • It reduces business disruption and limits damage from the attack.
  • Suggested Reading: Metadata for Incident Response: Strengthening Your Network Security Strategy

These strategies help businesses stay safer from malware and limit damage from attacks.

Bonus: Best Practices for a Stronger Defense

To further bolster your defenses against malware, consider these additional best practices:

1. Monitor Network Traffic for Unusual Activity:

Continuous network monitoring helps identify suspicious behavior early.

It involves:

  • Tracking traffic patterns
  • Flagging anomalies

Early detection enables quick action to prevent malware from escalating.

2. Segment Networks to Contain Malware:

Network segmentation helps contain malware infections.

It involves separating different parts of your network to:

  • Limit the spread of malware
  • Reduce the risk of widespread attacks

Segmentation makes it harder for malware to propagate across the network.

3. Review Physical and Digital Security Regularly:

Cybersecurity involves both digital and physical security. Regularly assess both to ensure comprehensive protection.

Key areas to review include:

  • Access controls
  • Device security
  • Digital security protocols

Continually update measures to stay ahead of emerging threats.

By using these best practices along with key security strategies and a strong cybersecurity tool, your organization can create a more effective defense against attacks.

items.title: Claude AI Exploits Linux Kernel Flaw to Execute Root Commands Without User Interaction
items.summary: Anthropic says an unreleased Claude research model wrote a working exploit for a critical Linux kernel bug, tracked as CVE-2026-98432. The exploit lets a remote attacker run commands as root with no login and no user action. Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team shared the finding on October 27, 2026, and the flaw is already patched upstream. Anthropic’s research post says this was a lab test and not a real-world incident. After a first prompt from a researcher, Claude wrote an exploit that targets Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener. Anthropic describes the root cause as a race condition that leads to a use-after-free bug in the kernel networking stack. A use-after-free happens when code keeps using memory after the system has already released it. Claude AI Exploits Critical Linux Kernel Flaw The exploit works in two steps. First, it abuses the race to make the kernel send back extra bytes, and one reply can contain a kernel pointer. That pointer reveals the memory layout and defeats KASLR, a defense that hides where kernel code sits. Second, the same bug overwrites a callback pointer so the kernel runs a payload the attacker already placed in memory, which ends in a shell command as root. Anthropic notes that a lost race only fails the TCP handshake and does not crash the machine. An attacker can therefore retry again and again. In the proof of concept, leaking the pointer took 48 minutes and running the command took five more. Our own earlier report on the full Claude exploit research covers the Chrome, Safari, Android and Windows chains from the same study. The public record looks a little different from Anthropic’s description. The Ubuntu entry for CVE-2026-98432 was published on October 15, 2026 and last updated on October 28. It carries a CVSS 3 score of 9.8, which is Critical, and an Ubuntu priority of High. The text describes an IPv4 fix named “free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period.” It explains that tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() hands IP options to a child socket without copying them. Another CPU can then process a repeated SYN and build a reply while the options are freed with a plain kfree(), which causes the use-after-free in ip_options_build(). The fix switches to kfree_rcu(), which delays the free until readers are done. The record says IPv6 is not hit by the first issue. The record never mentions multipath TCP. The link between the CVE and Anthropic’s Linux chain rests on Anthropic’s post, a gap that Cyber Security News also pointed out . Readers should treat the exact attack path as the vendor’s claim until others reproduce it. A threat summary from Aviatrix states the same caution, since no outside team has confirmed the chain end to end. Patch Status Anthropic says the bug was fixed upstream and backported to all maintained stable kernel branches. One security blog lists fixed stable releases such as 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113 and 6.18.56, though readers should confirm those numbers on kernel.org . Distribution fixes are uneven. At the time of writing, Ubuntu’s page marks 22.04, 24.04 and 26.04 kernels as vulnerable with work in progress, and older releases such as 20.04 and 18.04 as vulnerable. Many cloud kernels for AWS, Azure and GCP are also listed as affected. One patch guide reports that Oracle Linux has shipped fixed packages. Internet-facing servers should come first in any patch plan. The bigger story is speed. Anthropic argues that models can now find and chain bugs into working exploits with little human help. That work once needed a small group of expert teams. Defenders can use the same tools, and Anthropic points to its expanded Cyber Verification Program for approved security staff. AI is also moving into kernel work from the safe side. Linus Torvalds recently said Claude Code helped write Linux kernel patches , which shows the same tools help both builders and bug hunters. Install the latest kernel update from your distribution and reboot, since a kernel fix does not apply until the system restarts. If a patch is not ready, check whether you really need multipath TCP listeners and turn them off where you do not. Limit exposure of public services with firewall rules, and watch for odd resets or failed handshakes on listening ports. Teams that run AI tools should also review their own setups. We recently covered a Claude Cowork sandbox flaw that let an attacker reach root inside the product’s Linux sandbox. Scan your own code often, patch fast, and treat AI-found bugs as a sign that the gap between discovery and exploit is shrinking.

items.title: NIST Officially Released Guidance for Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography
items.summary: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has released guidance on moving to post-quantum cryptography , giving federal agencies and technology providers a clearer path to quantum-resistant security. Published October 27, 2026, the finalized report identifies vulnerable cryptographic standards, their replacements, and the timelines that should shape migration plans. The report, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards (NISTIR 8547), builds on the three standards NIST finalized in August 2024. Rather than introducing another algorithm, it explains how organizations should move away from cryptography that future quantum computers could break. A powerful enough quantum computer could threaten the cryptographic methods protecting sensitive communications and records. The immediate concern is “ harvest now, decrypt later ,” where attackers collect encrypted information today and store it until quantum technology can unlock it. Data that must remain private for many years faces particular risk. NIST mathematician Dustin Moody, who leads the agency’s PQC standardization project, said migration requirements differ across use cases. NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Guidance Organizations must account for their systems, suppliers, and operational needs instead of treating the transition as a single software update. National Security Memorandum 10 established 2035 as the main target for completing the federal transition. Executive Order 14412 brought forward deadlines for federal high-value assets and high-impact systems, requiring quantum-resistant key establishment by 2030 and digital signatures by 2031. These deadlines do not automatically apply to every private business. However, suppliers serving federal agencies should assess how customer requirements could affect their products and services. Cybersecurity News previously covered the White House’s federal post-quantum migration order . NIST’s standards separate two essential tasks. FIPS 203 defines ML-KEM for establishing shared secret keys. FIPS 204 and FIPS 205 define ML-DSA and SLH-DSA for digital signatures, which help verify authenticity and detect changes to signed information. These functions need separate migration planning. Organizations should identify where cryptography operates, assess supplier readiness, and prioritize systems that protect long-lived sensitive data. Related coverage of MITRE’s post-quantum cryptography migration roadmap explains why planning must begin before quantum computers become a practical threat. The report also allows hybrid approaches that combine conventional cryptography with post-quantum methods. This can provide an additional security margin, but it requires more computing resources. Teams must weigh that tradeoff against deployment needs. For implementation support, NIST points organizations toward its National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence migration project. Its work covers cryptographic visibility, risk-based priorities, and practical demonstrations. Together, these resources connect federal transition requirements with the technical work needed to replace vulnerable cryptography across products, services, and supply chains without relying on a single migration strategy. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

FIPS 204 and FIPS 205 define ML-DSA and SLH-DSA for digital signatures, which help verify authenticity and detect changes to signed information. These functions need separate migration planning.

Organizations should identify where cryptography operates, assess supplier readiness, and prioritize systems that protect long-lived sensitive data. Related coverage of MITRE’s post-quantum cryptography migration roadmap explains why planning must begin before quantum computers become a practical threat.

The report also allows hybrid approaches that combine conventional cryptography with post-quantum methods. This can provide an additional security margin, but it requires more computing resources. Teams must weigh that tradeoff against deployment needs.

For implementation support, NIST points organizations toward its National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence migration project. Its work covers cryptographic visibility, risk-based priorities, and practical demonstrations.

Together, these resources connect federal transition requirements with the technical work needed to replace vulnerable cryptography across products, services, and supply chains without relying on a single migration strategy.

items.title: Zero-Click ‘SMS of Death’ Flaw Lets Hackers Disrupt Android Phones With a Single Text
items.summary: A security researcher has published details of a zero-click Android flaw called “SMS of Death.” One malformed text message can crash the phone service on an Android device, drop active calls, and in the worst case leave the phone without telephony after every restart. Google has marked the report “Won’t Fix” and treats it as a non-security issue, according to the researcher’s disclosure site. The bug sits in WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu() , the Android code that reads WAP Push messages. These are special data texts that never show up in the inbox. The code reads a header length from the message as a long number and then converts it to a smaller signed integer without checking the range. The researcher shows that the five bytes 88 80 80 80 00 turn into -2147483648 after this conversion. Android then tries to create a byte array of that size. That throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException and kills the com.android.phone process. The victim sees nothing. No message appears, and the sender’s number stays hidden. Zero-Click ‘SMS of Death’ Flaw Active calls end with the cause CS_DEATH as the process restarts. Each message causes one to two seconds without service. The carrier also resends texts the phone never acknowledges, so one message caused repeated outages for up to a week in testing. About 20 messages left a phone unusable for a long time. The researcher tested a Pixel 9 on April 2026 firmware, and several Samsung Galaxy and A-series phones, and the crash happened every time. Android already has other zero-click risks from fake cell towers. Google’s Android 17 adds protections against 2G downgrade and SMS blaster tricks . Those protections target a different problem and do not appear to cover this parsing bug. Sending about 30 messages in quick succession is far worse. The repeated crashes collide with writes to the SMS store and corrupt the SQLite database that holds messages. After that, the phone app crashes on every boot, and a restart does not help. A factory reset only works for a short time, because the carrier sends the stuck payload again. The researcher’s fix was to move the physical SIM into a non-Android phone such as an iPhone so the carrier’s retries get acknowledged. Then the corrupt records had to be cleared over ADB. An eSIM would make recovery much harder, and most users could not do it. Zero-click attacks on phones are not new. In 2023, Citizen Lab found BLASTPASS, an iPhone zero-click chain used to install Pegasus spyware AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

That throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException and kills the com.android.phone process. The victim sees nothing. No message appears, and the sender’s number stays hidden.

items.title: Malicious Firefox extensions impersonate popular crypto wallets
items.summary: Socket’s threat researchers found three malicious Firefox extensions that impersonated the Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget crypto wallets. Once installed, the malicious extensions stole recovery phrases and private keys, which would provide the attacker with full control of a wallet. A crypto wallet is an app, browser extension, or physical device that lets you manage cryptocurrency such as Bitcoin. Despite its name, it doesn’t actually hold your coins. Those are recorded on a blockchain , a shared digital record of transactions. Instead, the wallet manages the secret digital keys that let you access and spend them. When you create a wallet, you may be given a recovery phrase: a list of words you can use to restore access. Write it down and store it offline. It’s a backup of your keys, not just an ordinary password. Anyone who gets hold of it can take control of your funds, which is why fake wallet extensions try to steal it. Cybercriminals listed three fake wallet extensions on Firefox Add-ons, impersonating Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget. The genuine wallets offer extensions for other browsers: Jupiter lists Chrome, Brave, and Edge; Bitget’s extension is for Chrome; and Phantom says its Firefox extension is no longer supported . The malicious extensions looked for 12-, 15-, 18-, and 24-word recovery phrases, as well as Ethereum and Solana private keys. They could read input fields, detect pasted text, and scan screens displaying recovery phrases. A recovery phrase or private key is a bearer secret: whoever holds it controls the wallet and can move its assets. The Phantom variant’s backend logged captured secrets, sent them to a Telegram bot , and automatically moved funds to hardcoded payout addresses. Those addresses covered Ethereum, BSC, Polygon, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, Avalanche, Solana, and Bitcoin. The Phantom variant could read a phrase both when it was typed during import and when it was displayed on a reveal screen. How to stay safe Socket says all three listings were live on Firefox Add-ons during its analysis and have since been removed. But if you find one of these extensions in your Firefox browser, you should: Remove the extension. Use the three-dot menu next to it and choose Remove . If you ever entered a phrase or key, create a new wallet on a clean device and move your assets immediately. Treat the old wallet as compromised. In the future, install wallets only from the vendor’s official website link, not from store search results. The fake Phantom listing asked to access data on all websites and had no privacy policy. These are warning signs to look out for. Use an up-to-date, real-time anti-malware solution that blocks malicious websites. Malwarebytes blocks bonto.io subdomains Never enter your recovery phrase on a website. Enter it only in the official wallet app when restoring. Wallet support will never ask for it. IOCs The malicious extensions: Phantom impersonator: add-on ID 3092199 Jupiter impersonator: add-on ID 3092666 Bitget impersonator: add-on ID 3092059 Subdomains: bonto[.]io phantom[.]bonto[.]io jupiter[.]bonto[.]io bitget[.]bonto[.]io coinbase[.]bonto[.]io exodus[.]bonto[.]io IP addresses: 104.21.34[.]69 172.67.155[.]198 From reporting threats to removing them. Cybersecurity risks should never spread beyond a headline. Keep threats off your devices by downloading Malwarebytes today .

items.title: How to Export Logs from OpenSearch
items.summary: Pull documents with the _search API, or let a short Python script page through them with helpers.scan. If your pipeline kept the original log line, usually in message or event.original, extract just that field and you get the raw logs back. OpenSearch Dashboards can generate reports from saved searches, but not in a format LogTotal reads today. OpenSearch backs a lot of homegrown SIEMs and log platforms, including Amazon OpenSearch Service and the Wazuh indexer. Prime Core has 23,466 detection rules for OpenSearch, mapped to 671 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get a clean slice of data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Permissions. With the security plugin enabled, your role needs read access on the index pattern: the read action group, or at least indices:data/read/search* and indices:data/read/scroll*. On Amazon OpenSearch Service, that’s either a fine-grained access control user or IAM credentials with SigV4 signing. Find the right fields. Index patterns differ between pipelines. Check one document and the mapping before you write a query: GET logs-*/_search?size=1 GET logs-*/_mapping You’re looking for the time field (@timestamp or timestamp) and, ideally, a field that holds the original line (message, event.original, full_log in Wazuh). Count first. Run GET logs-*/_count with the same query to see what you’re about to pull. The commands below follow the OpenSearch 2.x documentation, checked October 2026. Option 1: Python with opensearch-py (recommended) helpers.scan handles paging and cleans up after itself. Install opensearch-py, then: import json, os from opensearchpy import OpenSearch, helpers client = OpenSearch( "https://opensearch.example.com:9200", http_auth=("reader", os.environ["OS_PASSWORD"]), verify_certs=True, ) query = {"query": {"range": {"@timestamp": { "gte": "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z", "lt": "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"}}}} with open("opensearch_1019.jsonl", "w") as out: for hit in helpers.scan(client, index="logs-*", query=query, size=1000): out.write(json.dumps(hit["_source"]) + "\n") To get raw lines instead of documents, write hit[“_source”].get(“message”, “”) instead of the whole _source. To keep the file small, add “_source”: [“@timestamp”, “host.name”, “message”] to the query. Option 2: curl for small exports For up to 10,000 documents, one request is enough: curl -sS -u reader -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ "https://opensearch.example.com:9200/logs-*/_search" -d '{ "size": 10000, "query": {"range": {"@timestamp": {"gte": "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z", "lt": "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"}}}, "sort": [{"@timestamp": "asc"}] }' | jq -c '.hits.hits[]._source' > opensearch_small.jsonl 10,000 is the default index.max_result_window. Past that, the request fails, and you want Option 1, or a point in time (PIT) with search_after if you’d rather script it yourself. Step 3: Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Look it over before you continue. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix security_exception / 403 Role lacks search or scroll permissions Ask for read on the index pattern Result window is too large More than 10,000 hits in one request Use helpers.scan or PIT with search_after Zero hits, but the data is there Wrong time field name, or a time zone mix-up Check the mapping; use explicit Z timestamps No search context found Scroll expired between pages Pass scroll=”5m” to helpers.scan; use smaller pages Signature errors on Amazon OpenSearch Service IAM-based domain expects SigV4 Use AWSV4SignerAuth from opensearch-py FAQ Does this work for Wazuh? Yes. The Wazuh indexer is OpenSearch-based. Alerts usually live in wazuh-alerts-*, and the original log line in full_log. Should I export everything in _source? Only if you need it. Pipelines often add dozens of enrichment fields. Trimming to time, host and the raw message keeps files small and uploads fast.
items.summary_html:
Pull documents with the _search API, or let a short Python script page through them with helpers.scan. If your pipeline kept the original log line, usually in message or event.original, extract just that field and you get the raw logs back. OpenSearch Dashboards can generate reports from saved searches, but not in a format LogTotal reads today.

OpenSearch backs a lot of homegrown SIEMs and log platforms, including Amazon OpenSearch Service and the Wazuh indexer. Prime Core has 23,466 detection rules for OpenSearch, mapped to 671 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get a clean slice of data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

Permissions. With the security plugin enabled, your role needs read access on the index pattern: the read action group, or at least indices:data/read/search* and indices:data/read/scroll*. On Amazon OpenSearch Service, that’s either a fine-grained access control user or IAM credentials with SigV4 signing.

Find the right fields. Index patterns differ between pipelines. Check one document and the mapping before you write a query:

GET logs-*/_search?size=1
GET logs-*/_mapping

You’re looking for the time field (@timestamp or timestamp) and, ideally, a field that holds the original line (message, event.original, full_log in Wazuh).

Count first. Run GET logs-*/_count with the same query to see what you’re about to pull.

The commands below follow the OpenSearch 2.x documentation, checked October 2026.

Option 1: Python with opensearch-py (recommended)

helpers.scan handles paging and cleans up after itself. Install opensearch-py, then:

import json, os
from opensearchpy import OpenSearch, helpers

client = OpenSearch(
    "https://opensearch.example.com:9200",
    http_auth=("reader", os.environ["OS_PASSWORD"]),
    verify_certs=True,
)
query = {"query": {"range": {"@timestamp": {
    "gte": "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z", "lt": "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"}}}}

with open("opensearch_1019.jsonl", "w") as out:
    for hit in helpers.scan(client, index="logs-*", query=query, size=1000):
        out.write(json.dumps(hit["_source"]) + "\n")

To get raw lines instead of documents, write hit[“_source”].get(“message”, “”) instead of the whole _source. To keep the file small, add “_source”: [“@timestamp”, “host.name”, “message”] to the query.

Option 2: curl for small exports

For up to 10,000 documents, one request is enough:

curl -sS -u reader -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  "https://opensearch.example.com:9200/logs-*/_search" -d '{
    "size": 10000,
    "query": {"range": {"@timestamp": {"gte": "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z", "lt": "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"}}},
    "sort": [{"@timestamp": "asc"}]
  }' | jq -c '.hits.hits[]._source' > opensearch_small.jsonl

10,000 is the default index.max_result_window. Past that, the request fails, and you want Option 1, or a point in time (PIT) with search_after if you’d rather script it yourself.

Step 3: Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal
  1. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file.
  2. Sanitize. Look it over before you continue.
  3. Review. 
When it goes wrong SymptomLikely causeFixsecurity_exception / 403Role lacks search or scroll permissionsAsk for read on the index patternResult window is too largeMore than 10,000 hits in one requestUse helpers.scan or PIT with search_afterZero hits, but the data is thereWrong time field name, or a time zone mix-upCheck the mapping; use explicit Z timestampsNo search context foundScroll expired between pagesPass scroll=”5m” to helpers.scan; use smaller pagesSignature errors on Amazon OpenSearch ServiceIAM-based domain expects SigV4Use AWSV4SignerAuth from opensearch-py
FAQ

Does this work for Wazuh?

Yes. The Wazuh indexer is OpenSearch-based. Alerts usually live in wazuh-alerts-*, and the original log line in full_log.

Should I export everything in _source?

Only if you need it. Pipelines often add dozens of enrichment fields. Trimming to time, host and the raw message keeps files small and uploads fast.

items.title: Salt Security adds autonomous defence capabilities to agentic security platform
items.summary: Salt Security has announced Autonomous Defense for its Agentic Security Platform , expanding its Salt Workflows capabilities to automate threat containment, enforcement and remediation. The update enables security teams to trigger actions such as blocking malicious activity, revoking risky access and initiating configuration changes through existing enterprise tools. The announcement addresses the delay between detecting a threat and taking action. Salt says response processes often depend on manual handovers across disconnected systems, leaving risks unresolved while teams investigate alerts and raise tickets. As AI accelerates the discovery and exploitation of weaknesses, the company argues that these delays can increase exposure. “Security cannot move at ticket speed when attackers move at machine speed,” said Aner Gelman, VP Product at Salt Security. “Autonomous Defense turns Salt’s security intelligence into action, from blocking malicious activity and revoking risky access to enforcing protections through controls enterprises already use.” The capabilities draw on Salt’s Agentic Security Graph , which connects AI agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, tools and downstream APIs with information from source code, configurations, exposure and runtime behaviour. This context helps identify potentially dangerous paths through an organisation’s systems and informs the responses customers choose to automate. Through Salt Workflows and supported connected controls, security teams can disable unauthorised MCP connections, quarantine shadow tools and remove excessive privileges. They can also push blocking rules to web application firewalls and API gateways, update AI guardrail policies, or trigger configuration changes to address exposed APIs and missing rate limits. Customers determine which findings trigger immediate action and which changes require approval. They also select the enforcement points used, allowing teams to retain oversight of sensitive operations and maintain an audit trail. Ticketing, notifications and SIEM enrichment remain available as part of the response process. Salt has embedded a visual, drag-and-drop workflow builder into the platform, supported by more than 200 out-of-the-box connectors and a marketplace of Salt-built integrations. According to the company, workflows can span security, infrastructure, IT and collaboration systems without requiring customers to standardise on a single gateway, agent framework or response product. “An alert doesn’t stop an attack. Action does,” said Roey Eliyahu, co-founder and CEO of Salt Security. “Salt secures the entire agentic path, from AI agents and MCPs to downstream APIs. Autonomous Defense puts that intelligence to work, helping security teams stop attacks and close dangerous paths before they cause business impact.” Salt Workflows is available to Salt Security customers now. The company is migrating existing workflows to the new experience, with support for customer-specific requirements. Automated actions depend on customers’ policies and the capabilities of their connected enforcement tools.
