items.summary_html:
New York, New York, October 29th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Now available as a standalone solution, Quantum Trust Hub delivers cryptographic posture management and agility for enterprises to uncover risk exposure, drive remediation at scale, and accelerate quantum readiness.  

AppViewX, the leading identity security company built for the AI-powered and post-quantum enterprise, today announced new capabilities for Quantum Trust Hub, now available as a standalone solution to help enterprises discover cryptographic assets, assess quantum-related vulnerabilities, prioritize risks by business impact, and take decisive action through integrated remediation workflows.

The new capabilities include an agentless-first approach that leverages organizations’ existing security infrastructure to discover cryptographic assets without the additional overhead of agents and sensors.

Organizations can also upload Cryptographic Bills of Materials (CBOMs) and Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) from third-party tools to build a single, unified inventory of cryptographic assets, and initiate remediation planning and execution through existing ITSM solutions.  

As enterprises prepare for the transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), understanding where vulnerable cryptography exists across their environments is becoming increasingly critical.

NIST finalized its first PQC standards in 2024 and has outlined plans to begin phasing out RSA and ECC in 2030.

By that same year, Executive Order 14412 directs federal agencies to transition high-value assets and high-impact systems to PQC for key establishment, with PQC adoption for digital signatures to follow by the end of 2031.

Meeting these deadlines requires a comprehensive understanding of cryptographic exposure, yet traditional certificate inventories alone do not tell the full story.

Cryptographic exposure extends beyond certificates to TLS configurations, keys, and application code, making it difficult to assess true risk and know where to focus first. 

Addressing these challenges requires continuous visibility across multiple layers of cryptographic infrastructure. Quantum Trust Hub delivers this through a vendor-neutral approach, consolidating findings from existing security tools and third-party inventories.

By building a unified cryptographic inventory and extending visibility across certificates, TLS configurations, cipher suites, and code libraries, the platform gives security teams the cryptographic posture management foundation they need, enabling continuous assessment of exposure, risk-based remediation prioritization, and the cryptographic agility to respond quickly as threats and standards evolve.  

“The quantum transition is a complex undertaking that enterprises need to start preparing for now,” said Jennifer Glenn, research director at IDC.

“Recent attacks involving compromised cryptographic credentials and signing keys underscore the risks organizations already face today. With federal migration deadlines approaching and quantum computing potentially advancing faster than expected, understanding the full scope of cryptographic exposure will be essential to planning an effective response.” 

With the latest Quantum Trust Hub capabilities, enterprises can: 

  • Expand cryptographic discovery using existing security investments: Through a new integration with Qualys, alongside existing Tenable support, organizations can discover cryptographic assets and configurations using security tools already deployed across their environments. AppViewX’s agentless-first approach reduces cost and complexity while supporting deeper discovery when needed.  
  • Build a single, unified cryptographic inventory: CBOMs and SBOMs from third-party tools can be uploaded directly into the platform, consolidating findings from multiple discovery sources across certificates, TLS configurations, cipher suites, keys, and application code. This provides the foundation for true cryptographic posture management. 
  • Prioritize what matters most: Assets are classified as quantum-vulnerable or quantum-resistant. Business application context and NIST-aligned severity ratings enable organizations to surface the most critical remediation priorities to address first. Executive dashboards and continuous monitoring track posture and migration progress over time. 
  • Drive remediation through existing ITSM workflows: Cryptographic findings are sent directly to ServiceNow as ready-to-work tickets containing affected assets, identified risks, recommended fixes, and ownership information. Tickets are grouped by remediation scope, with status tracked end-to-end so teams can ensure findings translate into action, not just reports. 
  • Move faster with cryptographic agility: By maintaining a comprehensive, continuously updated inventory of cryptographic assets and their risk status, organizations can respond quickly to new vulnerabilities, policy changes, and evolving PQC standards, without having to scramble to understand their exposure from scratch. 

The expansion of Quantum Trust Hub reinforces AppViewX’s broader mission to secure machine and AI identities, credentials, and cryptography through a cohesive product portfolio as enterprises navigate the transition to post-quantum computing.

Quantum Trust Hub works alongside AppViewX’s CLM and SSH Key Lifecycle Management solutions to accelerate remediation of certificates or SSH keys that require replacement as part of a PQC assessment.

Additionally, AppViewX recently advanced its Agent Identity Security solution to discover, govern, and control the actions of AI agents at runtime while extending its core CLM and PKI products to issue cryptographically verifiable, quantum-resilient identities for AI agents, establishing an additional layer of trust as they access enterprise systems.

Together, these offerings provide enterprises with a more comprehensive approach to securing machine and agent identities while managing cryptographic risk across their environments.  

“The quantum clock is ticking, and enterprises cannot afford to wait until post-quantum migration becomes an immediate requirement to understand their exposure,” said Archit Lohokare, CEO of AppViewX.

“Certificates are only one part of the equation. Cryptographic risk extends across the identities, keys, protocols, and applications that underpin enterprise trust. With Quantum Trust Hub, we’re giving organizations the continuous visibility and risk intelligence needed to identify vulnerable cryptography, focus on their most critical exposures, and take a more proactive approach to quantum readiness.” 

To learn more about Quantum Trust Hub, watch AppViewX’s on-demand webinar, “The Quantum Readiness Clock Is Ticking: What to Do Now” or explore a 30-day quantum readiness assessment by talking to an AppViewX expert. 

About AppViewX    

AppViewX is the leading machine and agent identity security company built for the AI and quantum enterprise, bringing together discovery, automation, control, and intelligence.

The AVX Platform helps enterprises reduce risk by providing complete visibility and governance over every machine and AI agent identity, automating their lifecycle, controlling their access, and ensuring compliance at the speed business demands.   

Trusted by global enterprises across financial services, healthcare, and technology, AppViewX is recognized as a leader in the IDC MarketScape for Certificate Lifecycle Management and KuppingerCole’s Non-Human Identity Management Leadership Compass. For more information, users can visit appviewx.com.

items.title: How to Export Logs from Splunk for Security Analysis
items.summary: The short answer: run the search, click Export in the job toolbar under the search bar, and choose Raw Events, CSV or JSON . For a few thousand events, that’s all you need. For bigger pulls, skip the browser and use the splunk search CLI or the REST export endpoint. Both stream results instead of making Splunk Web build one huge file for you. Why export from Splunk at all, if the data is already indexed? Usually because someone outside your Splunk needs to look at it: an IR partner, a colleague on another team, or you, on a laptop, without writing SPL for an hour. Prime Core has 23,674 detection rules for Splunk mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. That’s a lot of detection logic you can run against a small slice of your data once it’s out. Below is how to get that slice, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free TL;DR Route Use it when What you need Splunk Web → Export One-off, small export, you already have the search open Search access to the index splunk search CLI You have a shell on a Splunk Enterprise search head OS access + Splunk credentials REST search/jobs/export Large exports, scripting, or Splunk Cloud Access to the management port (8089) + a token Before you start Three things decide which route works for you: where your Splunk runs, what your role can search, and whether you’re allowed to take the data out. Index access. You can only export what your role can search. If a search comes back empty but you know the data is there, check your role’s allowed indexes before you start rewriting SPL. Put index= in the search explicitly; don’t rely on default indexes. Splunk Cloud vs. Enterprise. On Splunk Cloud Platform there’s no shell, so the CLI route is out. The REST API isn’t on by default either: someone has to request access for your stack, and free trials can’t use it at all. Splunk Web export works everywhere. Permission to export. Raw logs carry usernames, hostnames, internal IPs, sometimes tokens in URLs. LogTotal sanitizes uploads before analysis, but your company’s data-handling policy still applies. Get the OK first. It takes five minutes, and you’ll want it in writing if this turns into an incident. The commands below follow Splunk’s current documentation for Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud Platform, checked in October 2026. Links to every page we used are at the end. Step 1: Scope the search before you export anything The most common mistake is exporting a whole index “just in case.” You end up with a file nobody wants to open. Decide what question you’re answering, then pin down index, sourcetype, host and time: index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure host=web-03 earliest=-24h@h latest=@h For Windows Security events collected by the Splunk Add-on for Windows in XML mode: index=wineventlog source="XmlWinEventLog:Security" host=dc-01 earliest=-24h@h latest=@h Two rules keep the export useful. Keep _raw. If the search ends with stats, table or chart, you’re exporting a summary, not logs, and Splunk Web will grey out the Raw Events format. Export events, not results. If you go with JSON, trim the extracted fields so the file doesn’t triple in size: ... | fields _time host source sourcetype _raw Use absolute time when it matters. earliest=-24h means something different every minute. If Splunk has to rerun your search during export (more on that below), a relative window can return a slightly different set of events. For anything incident-related, use exact timestamps. One thing to know about Windows data: Splunk doesn’t keep the original .evtx files. It indexes the rendered event text, XML or classic key=value. So what you export is that text, not a binary EVTX. Step 2a: Export from Splunk Web Fine for small, one-off exports when the search is already on your screen. Run the search and let the job finish. Exporting a running job just gets you a partial picture. Click Export (the download arrow) in the row of job actions under the search bar. Pick the format. Raw Events gives you the original log lines exactly as they were indexed, which is what you want for syslog-style sources like linux_secure. JSON keeps host, source and sourcetype next to each event. That helps when the export spans several hosts. Name the file something you’ll recognize next week, for example web-03_sshd_2026-10-19.log. Leave Number of Results empty to export everything the search returned. If you type 500, you get the first 500 and nothing tells you there were more. Click Export . A detail that confuses people: export works from the search job artifact, not from what you see in the browser. If Splunk didn’t keep every result with the job, the dialog warns that it will rerun the search first. That’s normal. It just takes longer, which is why the absolute time range from Step 1 matters. Very long exports can also hit the Splunk Web session timeout. If the export runs for minutes, switch to the CLI or REST. Step 2b: Export with the Splunk CLI (Enterprise only) If you have a shell on the search head, this is the fastest route and the easiest to script. Log in first, so your password doesn’t end up in shell history the way it would with -auth: $SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk login $SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk search \ 'index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure host=web-03 earliest="10/19/2026:00:00:00" latest="10/20/2026:00:00:00"' \ -preview 0 -maxout 0 -output rawdata > web-03_sshd.log What each flag does: -maxout 0 removes the cap. By default the CLI exports 100 events and stops without a word. If your file has exactly 100 lines, this is why, not a quiet host. -preview 0 keeps preview results out of the file. -output rawdata writes the original lines. Use -output json if you want structured events with metadata. You can also run the CLI against a remote search head with -uri https:// :8089, as long as the management port is reachable from where you are. Two quick sanity checks before you upload: wc -l web-03_sshd.log head -3 web-03_sshd.log For single-line sources like linux_secure, the line count should roughly match the event count Splunk Web shows for the same search. The first lines should look like log lines, not error messages. Step 2c: Stream results through the REST API This is the route for big exports, scheduled pulls and Splunk Cloud (once REST access is enabled for your stack). The export endpoint streams results while the search runs, so there’s no job to poll and no result pages to walk through. Use an authentication token instead of a username and password. You create one in Settings → Tokens , if your admin has token authentication turned on. export SPLUNK_TOKEN=' ' curl -sS \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $SPLUNK_TOKEN" \ https://sh01.example.com:8089/services/search/v2/jobs/export \ --data-urlencode search='search index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure host=web-03' \ -d earliest_time='2026-10-19T00:00:00.000+00:00' \ -d latest_time='2026-10-20T00:00:00.000+00:00' \ -d output_mode=raw \ -o web-03_sshd.log Things that trip people up: The search string has to start with search (or a generating command such as | tstats). Paste your query without it and Splunk rejects it. output_mode=raw gives you the original lines, and it’s the fastest mode. output_mode=json streams one JSON object per line, with the event sitting under a result key. If you only want the events themselves, strip the envelope with jq: jq -c ‘select(.result) | .result’ export.json > events.ndjson. For a LogTotal upload, stick with raw. Lab instances often use self-signed certificates, and every Stack Overflow answer will tell you to add -k. In production, point curl at your CA with –cacert instead. If you POST to search/v2/jobs and read from /results, the server caps rows per request, and you have to page with offset. export doesn’t, which is the reason to use it here. Step 3: Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal LogTotal is SOC Prime’s free service for running detection logic against a log file without setting anything up. It sanitizes what you upload and doesn’t keep your files. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file from Step 2. Sanitize. Look it over before you continue. You know your environment better than any masking rule does. Review. When the export goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix CLI file has exactly 100 events Default -maxout is 100 Add -maxout 0 Raw Events is greyed out in the Export dialog The search ends in a transforming command (stats, table, chart) Export the events instead, or choose JSON Search returns nothing, but the data is there Index isn’t in your role’s allowed or default indexes, or wrong time range Add index= explicitly; ask your admin about the role Dialog says the search will be rerun The job artifact didn’t keep every result Expected behavior; use an absolute time range so the rerun returns the same events Browser export stalls or the file is cut short Splunk Web session timeout on a long export Switch to the CLI or REST 401 Unauthorized from curl Token expired, disabled, or token auth is off Create a new token in Settings → Tokens curl hangs or gets connection refused on 8089 Management port blocked, or REST not enabled on Splunk Cloud Check firewall rules; request REST access for your Cloud stack REST returns a search syntax error The query doesn’t start with search Prefix it with search JSON file is far bigger than expected Every extracted field got exported Add | fields _time host source sourcetype _raw FAQ Can I export logs from Splunk Cloud? Yes. Splunk Web export works the same as on Enterprise. The REST export endpoint works once API access is enabled for your stack; free trials don’t get it. The CLI isn’t an option, because there’s no shell on Splunk Cloud. Can I get the original EVTX files back out of Splunk? No. Splunk stores the rendered event text, not the binary .evtx. You can export that text as raw events or JSON. For real EVTX files, export them from the Windows host itself. Raw Events or JSON: which one should I pick for LogTotal? Raw. You get the same lines that sit on the host, and LogTotal reads syslog-format files as they are. JSON wraps each event in Splunk’s own structure. It’s handy when you need host and sourcetype next to every event, but for a LogTotal upload, raw is the safer choice. Is it safe to upload a Splunk export to an online tool? LogTotal sanitizes uploads before analysis and doesn’t retain files. How many events can I export? On the Splunk side, as many as you like: leave Number of Results empty in Splunk Web, or set -maxout 0 in the CLI. In practice, the limit is the upload size on the other end. So it pays to scope the search properly in Step 1.

The commands below follow Splunk’s current documentation for Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud Platform, checked in October 2026. Links to every page we used are at the end.

Step 1: Scope the search before you export anything

The most common mistake is exporting a whole index “just in case.” You end up with a file nobody wants to open. Decide what question you’re answering, then pin down index, sourcetype, host and time:

index=wineventlog source="XmlWinEventLog:Security" host=dc-01 earliest=-24h@h latest=@h

Two rules keep the export useful.

Keep _raw. If the search ends with stats, table or chart, you’re exporting a summary, not logs, and Splunk Web will grey out the Raw Events format. Export events, not results. If you go with JSON, trim the extracted fields so the file doesn’t triple in size:

... | fields _time host source sourcetype _raw

Use absolute time when it matters. earliest=-24h means something different every minute. If Splunk has to rerun your search during export (more on that below), a relative window can return a slightly different set of events. For anything incident-related, use exact timestamps.

One thing to know about Windows data: Splunk doesn’t keep the original .evtx files. It indexes the rendered event text, XML or classic key=value. So what you export is that text, not a binary EVTX.

Step 2a: Export from Splunk Web

Fine for small, one-off exports when the search is already on your screen.

  1. Run the search and let the job finish. Exporting a running job just gets you a partial picture.
  2. Click Export (the download arrow) in the row of job actions under the search bar.
  3. Pick the format. Raw Events gives you the original log lines exactly as they were indexed, which is what you want for syslog-style sources like linux_secure. JSON keeps host, source and sourcetype next to each event. That helps when the export spans several hosts.
  4. Name the file something you’ll recognize next week, for example web-03_sshd_2026-10-19.log.
  5. Leave Number of Results empty to export everything the search returned. If you type 500, you get the first 500 and nothing tells you there were more.
  6. Click Export.

A detail that confuses people: export works from the search job artifact, not from what you see in the browser. If Splunk didn’t keep every result with the job, the dialog warns that it will rerun the search first. That’s normal. It just takes longer, which is why the absolute time range from Step 1 matters. Very long exports can also hit the Splunk Web session timeout. If the export runs for minutes, switch to the CLI or REST.

Step 2b: Export with the Splunk CLI (Enterprise only)

If you have a shell on the search head, this is the fastest route and the easiest to script. Log in first, so your password doesn’t end up in shell history the way it would with -auth:

$SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk login

$SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk search \
  'index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure host=web-03 earliest="10/19/2026:00:00:00" latest="10/20/2026:00:00:00"' \
  -preview 0 -maxout 0 -output rawdata > web-03_sshd.log

What each flag does:

  • -maxout 0 removes the cap. By default the CLI exports 100 events and stops without a word. If your file has exactly 100 lines, this is why, not a quiet host.
  • -preview 0 keeps preview results out of the file.
  • -output rawdata writes the original lines. Use -output json if you want structured events with metadata.

You can also run the CLI against a remote search head with -uri https://:8089, as long as the management port is reachable from where you are.

Two quick sanity checks before you upload:

wc -l web-03_sshd.log
head -3 web-03_sshd.log

For single-line sources like linux_secure, the line count should roughly match the event count Splunk Web shows for the same search. The first lines should look like log lines, not error messages.

Step 2c: Stream results through the REST API

This is the route for big exports, scheduled pulls and Splunk Cloud (once REST access is enabled for your stack). The export endpoint streams results while the search runs, so there’s no job to poll and no result pages to walk through.

Use an authentication token instead of a username and password. You create one in Settings → Tokens, if your admin has token authentication turned on.

export SPLUNK_TOKEN=''

curl -sS \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SPLUNK_TOKEN" \
  https://sh01.example.com:8089/services/search/v2/jobs/export \
  --data-urlencode search='search index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure host=web-03' \
  -d earliest_time='2026-10-19T00:00:00.000+00:00' \
  -d latest_time='2026-10-20T00:00:00.000+00:00' \
  -d output_mode=raw \
  -o web-03_sshd.log

Things that trip people up:

  • The search string has to start with search (or a generating command such as | tstats). Paste your query without it and Splunk rejects it.
  • output_mode=raw gives you the original lines, and it’s the fastest mode. output_mode=json streams one JSON object per line, with the event sitting under a result key. If you only want the events themselves, strip the envelope with jq: jq -c ‘select(.result) | .result’ export.json > events.ndjson. For a LogTotal upload, stick with raw.
  • Lab instances often use self-signed certificates, and every Stack Overflow answer will tell you to add -k. In production, point curl at your CA with –cacert instead.
  • If you POST to search/v2/jobs and read from /results, the server caps rows per request, and you have to page with offset. export doesn’t, which is the reason to use it here.
Step 3: Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal

LogTotal is SOC Prime’s free service for running detection logic against a log file without setting anything up. It sanitizes what you upload and doesn’t keep your files.

  1. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file from Step 2. 
  2. Sanitize. Look it over before you continue. You know your environment better than any masking rule does.
  3. Review.

No. Splunk stores the rendered event text, not the binary .evtx. You can export that text as raw events or JSON. For real EVTX files, export them from the Windows host itself.

items.title: Hackers Exploit Critical Cisco SD-WAN 0-Day Flaw to Deploy KeyDrift Malware and Steal Encryption Keys
items.summary: A state-linked hacking group used a maximum-severity Cisco SD-WAN zero-day flaw to break into network controllers and install a custom malware framework called KeyDrift. The flaw is CVE-2026-20127. It carries a CVSS score of 10.0 and lets a remote attacker skip authentication and gain administrative rights without a password. KeyDrift is built to sit quietly inside the control system of a Cisco SD-WAN network. It copies the keys that protect traffic between company sites, and it also works as a backdoor. The targets named so far include space and satellite services, defense and aerospace companies, and policy research groups. Researchers from Cisco Talos identified the malware and published their findings on October 28, 2026. Talos tracks the actor as UAT-11473 and calls it a highly sophisticated advanced persistent threat (APT) group. It describes the activity as historical. It does not say when the intrusions happened or whether any stolen keys were actually sent out. Hackers Exploit Critical Cisco SD-WAN 0-Day Flaw The flaw sits in the peering authentication of the Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, Manager and Validator. An attacker sends crafted requests and logs in as a high-privileged internal user, which opens the door to NETCONF and lets them change the network setup. Cisco says no workaround exists, so patching is the only fix. Researchers later published a public proof-of-concept exploit for the same bug, which raised the risk for unpatched systems. After getting in, the attackers edit the startup scripts, known as runit service paths, so the malware starts with normal services. A script named conf_sshd finds the running vdaemon processes, and a tool called rsshd injects the main module into each one. conf_sshd control flow logic (Source – Cisco Talos) That module is PolyFlame. It lives only in memory and acts as a backdoor that can run commands and read or write files. It can also relay orders to other infected machines. One variant pretends to be the legitimate aaamgr service and uses anti-debugging checks to hide. The second module, LittleFilch, does the key theft. It hooks a function called SSL_read inside vdaemon and reads control messages after they are decrypted. For a preset list of edge routers, it grabs IP addresses and a 32-byte field that Talos believes is AES-256 key material for IPsec traffic. LittleFilch encrypts the haul with RSA, saves it to a file, and can send it out over UDP to an address in a config file that it deletes after reading. Links to Volt Typhoon and How to Defend Talos says with high confidence that UAT-11473’s infrastructure overlaps heavily with “Silent Train,” a covert access network linked to Volt Typhoon. items.summary_html:
A state-linked hacking group used a maximum-severity Cisco SD-WAN zero-day flaw to break into network controllers and install a custom malware framework called KeyDrift.

The flaw is CVE-2026-20127. It carries a CVSS score of 10.0 and lets a remote attacker skip authentication and gain administrative rights without a password.

KeyDrift is built to sit quietly inside the control system of a Cisco SD-WAN network. It copies the keys that protect traffic between company sites, and it also works as a backdoor.

The targets named so far include space and satellite services, defense and aerospace companies, and policy research groups. Researchers from Cisco Talos identified the malware and published their findings on October 28, 2026.

Talos tracks the actor as UAT-11473 and calls it a highly sophisticated advanced persistent threat (APT) group. It describes the activity as historical. It does not say when the intrusions happened or whether any stolen keys were actually sent out.

Hackers Exploit Critical Cisco SD-WAN 0-Day Flaw

The flaw sits in the peering authentication of the Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, Manager and Validator. An attacker sends crafted requests and logs in as a high-privileged internal user, which opens the door to NETCONF and lets them change the network setup.

Cisco says no workaround exists, so patching is the only fix. Researchers later published a public proof-of-concept exploit for the same bug, which raised the risk for unpatched systems.

After getting in, the attackers edit the startup scripts, known as runit service paths, so the malware starts with normal services. A script named conf_sshd finds the running vdaemon processes, and a tool called rsshd injects the main module into each one.

conf_sshd control flow logic (Source – Cisco Talos)

That module is PolyFlame. It lives only in memory and acts as a backdoor that can run commands and read or write files. It can also relay orders to other infected machines. One variant pretends to be the legitimate aaamgr service and uses anti-debugging checks to hide.

The second module, LittleFilch, does the key theft. It hooks a function called SSL_read inside vdaemon and reads control messages after they are decrypted.

For a preset list of edge routers, it grabs IP addresses and a 32-byte field that Talos believes is AES-256 key material for IPsec traffic.

LittleFilch encrypts the haul with RSA, saves it to a file, and can send it out over UDP to an address in a config file that it deletes after reading.

Links to Volt Typhoon and How to Defend

Talos says with high confidence that UAT-11473’s infrastructure overlaps heavily with “Silent Train,” a covert access network linked to Volt Typhoon.

That group has a record of hijacking routers, and earlier reporting on Volt Typhoon targeting Cisco routers shows how it turns edge devices into hidden relay points.

Cisco fixed CVE-2026-20127 in February 2026, so the first step is to confirm every controller runs a patched build. The first fixed releases are 20.9.8.2, 20.12.6.1, 20.15.4.2 and 20.18.2.1, depending on your release train.

conf_sshd execution logic (Source – Cisco Talos)

Versions older than 20.9 must move to a supported release. Until you upgrade, limit ports 22 and 830 to known controller addresses, but remember this does not remove malware that is already there.

Patching alone is not enough if you were exposed earlier. Check /var/log/auth.log for “Accepted publickey for vmanage-admin” entries from unknown IP addresses, and look for the files listed below.

Run “request admin-tech” on each control component before opening a Cisco TAC case. Defenders should also watch for a newer SD-WAN Controller flaw, CVE-2026-20182, which uses the same vdaemon service and was also exploited. For full guidance, see the Cisco security advisory.

items.title: How to Export Events from IBM QRadar
items.summary: The cleanest way to get raw events out of QRadar is the Ariel REST API. Run an AQL query that selects UTF8(payload), wait for the search to finish, and pull the results as JSON. You end up with the original log lines exactly as your log sources sent them. The Log Activity tab can export search results too, but not in a format LogTotal reads today. QRadar sits at the center of a lot of SOCs, and sooner or later someone needs a slice of its data outside the console: an IR partner, a second opinion, a quick check without building a new rule. Prime Core has 23,656 detection rules for QRadar, mapped to 674 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to pull a clean slice of raw events, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. This guide covers QRadar SIEM, on-premises and software. If your company was on QRadar SaaS, which IBM sold to Palo Alto Networks in 2024, you may have moved to Cortex XSIAM since. Get Started For Free Before you start An authorized service token. Create one under Admin → Authorized Services and give it an expiry date. The token carries a user role and a security profile. The security profile decides which log sources and networks it can see. If it’s narrower than your own, the API quietly returns fewer events than Log Activity shows you. That’s the most common “where did my events go?” moment with QRadar exports. Retention. Events live as long as your retention buckets allow ( Admin → Event Retention ). If the window you need is older than that, there’s nothing left to export. Network access. The API runs on the console’s HTTPS port. Consoles often use self-signed certificates; point curl at the right CA with –cacert rather than switching verification off. Step 1: Write the AQL query Select the payload plus a few fields for context: SELECT DATEFORMAT(starttime, 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss') AS event_time, LOGSOURCENAME(logsourceid) AS log_source, QIDNAME(qid) AS event_name, UTF8(payload) AS payload FROM events WHERE LOGSOURCENAME(logsourceid) = 'web-03' START '2026-10-19 00:00' STOP '2026-10-20 00:00' A few notes from experience: UTF8(payload) is the important part. Without it, the payload comes back as encoded bytes, not readable log text. Narrow it. Filter by log source name, or by type with LOGSOURCETYPENAME(devicetype) ILIKE ‘%Linux%’, and keep the window tight. START / STOP for exact windows , LAST 24 HOURS for relative ones. Test it first in Log Activity → Advanced Search . It’s the same AQL, and you’ll see the event count before you export. Windows events collected through WinCollect arrive as text payloads, not as EVTX. What you export is that text. Step 2: Run it through the Ariel API Save this as qradar_export.sh. It starts the search, waits for it, and writes one raw payload per line: #!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail QRADAR="https://qradar.example.com" TOKEN="${QRADAR_TOKEN:?set QRADAR_TOKEN first}" AQL="SELECT UTF8(payload) AS payload FROM events WHERE LOGSOURCENAME(logsourceid) = 'web-03' START '2026-10-19 00:00' STOP '2026-10-20 00:00'" # 1. start the search (-G puts the query in the URL, -X POST keeps the method) SID=$(curl -sS -G -X POST -H "SEC: $TOKEN" -H "Accept: application/json" \ --data-urlencode "query_expression=$AQL" \ "$QRADAR/api/ariel/searches" | jq -r '.search_id') # 2. wait for it to finish while :; do STATUS=$(curl -sS -H "SEC: $TOKEN" "$QRADAR/api/ariel/searches/$SID" | jq -r '.status') [ "$STATUS" = "COMPLETED" ] && break if [ "$STATUS" = "ERROR" ] || [ "$STATUS" = "CANCELED" ]; then echo "Search $STATUS"; exit 1; fi sleep 5 done # 3. fetch results: raw payloads, one per line curl -sS -H "SEC: $TOKEN" -H "Accept: application/json" \ "$QRADAR/api/ariel/searches/$SID/results" | jq -r '.events[].payload' > web-03_qradar_1019.log Want structured events instead, with time and log source as fields? Select those columns in the AQL and use jq -c ‘.events[]’ in the last step. You get one JSON object per line. For very large result sets, fetch the results in pages with a Range header, for example -H “Range: items=0-49999”, then the next 50,000. Step 3: Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Sanitize. Look it over before you continue. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix 401 from the API Token invalid, expired, or the SEC header is missing Check the header; create a new token Fewer events than Log Activity shows The token’s security profile sees fewer log sources Give the token a profile that matches the investigation Payloads look like encoded gibberish UTF8() left out of the query Select UTF8(payload) Search status goes to ERROR AQL syntax Test the query in Advanced Search first Results are empty Window is outside retention, or the time zone is off Check retention; check the console’s time zone curl complains about the certificate Self-signed console certificate Use –cacert with the console’s CA FAQ Can I get EVTX files out of QRadar? No. QRadar stores Windows events as text payloads. For real EVTX files, export them from the Windows host. What about flow data? Flows live in a separate table: query FROM flows instead of FROM events. They’re network connection records, not logs, and they’re a separate analysis.
items.summary_html:
The cleanest way to get raw events out of QRadar is the Ariel REST API. Run an AQL query that selects UTF8(payload), wait for the search to finish, and pull the results as JSON. You end up with the original log lines exactly as your log sources sent them. The Log Activity tab can export search results too, but not in a format LogTotal reads today. 

QRadar sits at the center of a lot of SOCs, and sooner or later someone needs a slice of its data outside the console: an IR partner, a second opinion, a quick check without building a new rule. Prime Core has 23,656 detection rules for QRadar, mapped to 674 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to pull a clean slice of raw events, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal.

This guide covers QRadar SIEM, on-premises and software. If your company was on QRadar SaaS, which IBM sold to Palo Alto Networks in 2024, you may have moved to Cortex XSIAM since.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

An authorized service token. Create one under Admin → Authorized Services and give it an expiry date. The token carries a user role and a security profile. The security profile decides which log sources and networks it can see. If it’s narrower than your own, the API quietly returns fewer events than Log Activity shows you. That’s the most common “where did my events go?” moment with QRadar exports.

Retention. Events live as long as your retention buckets allow (Admin → Event Retention). If the window you need is older than that, there’s nothing left to export.

Network access. The API runs on the console’s HTTPS port. Consoles often use self-signed certificates; point curl at the right CA with –cacert rather than switching verification off.

Step 1: Write the AQL query

Select the payload plus a few fields for context:

SELECT DATEFORMAT(starttime, 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss') AS event_time,
       LOGSOURCENAME(logsourceid) AS log_source,
       QIDNAME(qid) AS event_name,
       UTF8(payload) AS payload
FROM events
WHERE LOGSOURCENAME(logsourceid) = 'web-03'
START '2026-10-19 00:00' STOP '2026-10-20 00:00'

A few notes from experience:

  • UTF8(payload) is the important part. Without it, the payload comes back as encoded bytes, not readable log text.
  • Narrow it. Filter by log source name, or by type with LOGSOURCETYPENAME(devicetype) ILIKE ‘%Linux%’, and keep the window tight.
  • START / STOP for exact windows, LAST 24 HOURS for relative ones.
  • Test it first in Log Activity → Advanced Search. It’s the same AQL, and you’ll see the event count before you export.

Windows events collected through WinCollect arrive as text payloads, not as EVTX. What you export is that text.

Step 2: Run it through the Ariel API

Save this as qradar_export.sh. It starts the search, waits for it, and writes one raw payload per line:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

QRADAR="https://qradar.example.com"
TOKEN="${QRADAR_TOKEN:?set QRADAR_TOKEN first}"
AQL="SELECT UTF8(payload) AS payload FROM events WHERE LOGSOURCENAME(logsourceid) = 'web-03' START '2026-10-19 00:00' STOP '2026-10-20 00:00'"

# 1. start the search (-G puts the query in the URL, -X POST keeps the method)
SID=$(curl -sS -G -X POST -H "SEC: $TOKEN" -H "Accept: application/json" \
  --data-urlencode "query_expression=$AQL" \
  "$QRADAR/api/ariel/searches" | jq -r '.search_id')

# 2. wait for it to finish
while :; do
  STATUS=$(curl -sS -H "SEC: $TOKEN" "$QRADAR/api/ariel/searches/$SID" | jq -r '.status')
  [ "$STATUS" = "COMPLETED" ] && break
  if [ "$STATUS" = "ERROR" ] || [ "$STATUS" = "CANCELED" ]; then echo "Search $STATUS"; exit 1; fi
  sleep 5
done

# 3. fetch results: raw payloads, one per line
curl -sS -H "SEC: $TOKEN" -H "Accept: application/json" \
  "$QRADAR/api/ariel/searches/$SID/results" | jq -r '.events[].payload' > web-03_qradar_1019.log

Want structured events instead, with time and log source as fields? Select those columns in the AQL and use jq -c ‘.events[]’ in the last step. You get one JSON object per line.

For very large result sets, fetch the results in pages with a Range header, for example -H “Range: items=0-49999”, then the next 50,000.

Step 3: Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal
  1. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. 
  2. Sanitize. Look it over before you continue.
  3. Review. 
When it goes wrong SymptomLikely causeFix401 from the APIToken invalid, expired, or the SEC header is missingCheck the header; create a new tokenFewer events than Log Activity showsThe token’s security profile sees fewer log sourcesGive the token a profile that matches the investigationPayloads look like encoded gibberishUTF8() left out of the querySelect UTF8(payload)Search status goes to ERRORAQL syntaxTest the query in Advanced Search firstResults are emptyWindow is outside retention, or the time zone is offCheck retention; check the console’s time zonecurl complains about the certificateSelf-signed console certificateUse –cacert with the console’s CA
FAQ

Can I get EVTX files out of QRadar?

No. QRadar stores Windows events as text payloads. For real EVTX files, export them from the Windows host.

What about flow data?

Flows live in a separate table: query FROM flows instead of FROM events. They’re network connection records, not logs, and they’re a separate analysis.

items.title: CVE-2026-108142: Critical Veeam Backup & Replication Authorization Bypass
items.summary: Veeam has released security updates to address CVE-2026-108142, a critical authorization bypass vulnerability affecting Veeam Backup & Replication 13. The flaw allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass authorization controls associated with the Veeam CDP Coordinator Service. The vulnerability carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.1 and affects both Windows-based Veeam Backup & Replication deployments and the Veeam Software Appliance. Veeam disclosed the issue on October 27, 2026 as part of security advisory KB4948. Backup infrastructure is an especially sensitive security target because it contains recovery data and often has privileged connectivity to production systems. An authorization weakness affecting a central backup component therefore warrants immediate attention even though the vendor has not publicly documented the complete exploitation chain. Veeam’s CVSS vector identifies network-based exploitation with low attack complexity, no privileges required, and no user interaction. However, the vector also specifies that additional attack requirements must be present. Veeam has not publicly explained those prerequisites. The vulnerability affects Veeam Backup & Replication 13.1.1.18 and all earlier builds in the 13.1 branch, as well as version 13.0.2.29 and all earlier 13.0 builds. Veeam explicitly states that older releases such as version 12.x are not affected by this specific flaw. For CVE-2026-108142 detection, security teams should prioritize identifying vulnerable Backup & Replication installations and monitoring the backup server for unexpected activity involving the CDP Coordinator Service, unauthorized configuration changes, suspicious backup infrastructure modifications, and network connections from untrusted systems. SOC Prime users can strengthen visibility into vulnerability exploitation and post-compromise activity by correlating network, endpoint, identity, and application telemetry with behavior-based detection content. Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and hunting logic. To Detect CVE-2026-108142, defenders should combine vulnerability inventory with monitoring of Veeam services, administrative activity, system changes, and network access to backup infrastructure. Contact Sales CVE-2026-108142 analysis The vulnerability is located in the Veeam CDP Coordinator Service, a component of Veeam Backup & Replication responsible for coordinating Continuous Data Protection operations. According to Veeam documentation, the CDP Coordinator Service runs on the backup server and communicates with VMware vCenter, assigns CDP tasks, manages infrastructure components involved in Continuous Data Protection, and coordinates replication and data transfer operations. This makes authorization controls around the service particularly important. The backup server acts as the configuration and management core of the backup infrastructure, while the CDP Coordinator Service can interact with infrastructure components involved in replication. The details for CVE-2026-108142 remain intentionally limited in the public disclosure. Veeam describes the vulnerability as allowing an unauthenticated attacker to bypass authorization on the CDP Coordinator Service but does not disclose the vulnerable request, affected function, protocol interaction, exploitation sequence, or underlying implementation defect. The CVE is categorized as CWE-636, Not Failing Securely, commonly described as a “fail-open” condition. This weakness class occurs when a security mechanism encounters an error or unexpected state and falls into a less secure condition instead of denying access. However, the CWE classification alone should not be used to infer the precise implementation error in Veeam’s software. The vendor has not published enough technical information to determine exactly how the authorization bypass is triggered. The CVSS v4.0 vector is: CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:H/SA:H This indicates: Network-based attack vector Low attack complexity Additional attack requirements present No privileges required No user interaction required No direct confidentiality impact identified High integrity and availability impact High integrity and availability impact on subsequent systems That final distinction is important. Veeam’s scoring suggests that successful exploitation could affect not only the vulnerable backup system but also systems downstream from it. However, the vendor has not described exactly what operations an attacker can perform after bypassing authorization. Neither Veeam nor the supplied reports state that the vulnerability provides arbitrary remote code execution. CybersecurityNews specifically notes that the advisory does not describe an attack sequence or say that the flaw enables RCE. CyberPress likewise states that Veeam has not published exploitation steps or claimed code execution. Therefore, claims that the flaw directly provides shell access, SYSTEM privileges, credential theft, or arbitrary command execution would currently go beyond the available evidence. CVE-2026-108142 affects two Veeam Backup & Replication 13 branches: Version 13.1.1.18 and earlier 13.1 builds Version 13.0.2.29 and earlier 13.0 builds The vulnerability applies to both Windows-based Veeam Backup & Replication installations and Veeam Software Appliance deployments. Veeam Backup & Replication 12.x and other older releases identified by the vendor are not affected by this particular issue. Organizations should verify the exact build rather than relying solely on the major version number. For example, an installation reporting version 13.1 may still be vulnerable unless it has been upgraded to build 13.1.2.57 or later. Administrators can review their installed Backup & Replication build from the product interface and compare it with Veeam’s release information. At the time of writing, no public CVE-2026-108142 PoC has been documented by Veeam or the supplied security reports. Independent public vulnerability tracking also reports no openly available proof-of-concept exploit. Veeam has likewise not reported active exploitation of the vulnerability. This distinction is particularly relevant because Veeam infrastructure has been targeted through other vulnerabilities in previous attacks. CybersecurityNews notes prior exploitation of CVE-2024-40711 in ransomware operations, but that historical activity does not demonstrate exploitation of the newly disclosed authorization bypass. As of October 29, 2026, the new CVE is also not listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog according to currently available vulnerability tracking data. There are therefore no confirmed campaign-specific CVE-2026-108142 IOCs such as malicious IP addresses, domains, hashes, exploit payloads, or known attacker infrastructure associated with this vulnerability. Security teams should instead focus on exposure assessment and behavioral monitoring. Potential investigation points include: Network connections to Veeam backup infrastructure from unexpected systems Unexpected interaction with the CDP Coordinator Service Unauthorized changes to backup or CDP configuration New or modified backup jobs without an administrative explanation Unexpected service restarts or failures Changes to replication policies Modifications to protected infrastructure that do not correspond with approved administrative activity Suspicious account or privilege changes on the backup server Unexpected processes or network activity originating from Veeam infrastructure Attempts to reach backup management services from user networks or internet-facing systems These behaviors are not vulnerability-specific indicators. They are defensive hunting opportunities that may help uncover suspicious activity involving a critical backup server while technical exploitation details remain unavailable. Organizations should also review network segmentation around Veeam infrastructure. Backup servers should not be broadly reachable from ordinary workstations, guest environments, or untrusted network segments. Only systems that require communication with Veeam services should be permitted to reach the relevant interfaces and ports. This reduces the number of systems capable of interacting with a vulnerable service while patches are being deployed. The October security update also addresses three additional vulnerabilities. CVE-2026-108140 and CVE-2026-108141 are medium-severity relative path traversal vulnerabilities rated CVSS 5.9. Exploitation requires an authenticated Restore Operator who also controls the contents of a backed-up NAS share. Under those conditions, attacker-controlled files can be written to arbitrary locations on the backup server. A separate issue, CVE-2026-105477, affects Veeam Agent for Linux installations managed by Backup & Replication. The high-severity vulnerability can enable local privilege escalation and is fixed in Veeam Agent for Linux 13.1.2, build 13.1.2.11. Organizations applying the October updates should therefore review their entire Veeam environment rather than addressing only the critical authorization bypass. CVE-2026-108142 Mitigation The primary remediation is to install the fixed Veeam Backup & Replication releases. For the 13.1 branch, upgrade to: Veeam Backup & Replication 13.1.2 — build 13.1.2.57 For the 13.0 branch, upgrade to: Veeam Backup & Replication 13.0.3 — build 13.0.3.63 These builds contain the vendor-provided fix for the authorization vulnerability. The recommended CVE-2026-108142 mitigation process should begin with identifying every Veeam Backup & Replication server and determining its exact installed build. Security teams should prioritize upgrades for backup servers that are accessible across large network segments, connected to critical virtualization infrastructure, or supporting high-value production workloads. The patch should be treated as a security priority because exploitation requires no authenticated account according to the published CVSS vector. Veeam has not published a complete workaround in KB4948 that eliminates the vulnerability without installing the fixed software. If an immediate upgrade is operationally impossible, organizations should apply defense-in-depth measures until patching can be completed: Restrict access to Veeam backup servers using network segmentation. Permit connections only from systems that legitimately require access. Block unnecessary communication from workstation and user VLANs. Prevent direct internet exposure of backup infrastructure. Apply host-based firewall restrictions where operationally appropriate. Monitor access to Veeam services from unexpected systems. Review administrative and backup configuration changes. Monitor the backup server for unusual process execution or outbound connections. Protect administrative credentials using strong authentication and least privilege. Maintain immutable or offline backup copies where possible. These controls reduce attack surface but should not be considered substitutes for the vendor update. Veeam’s release information states that 13.1.2.57 is a cumulative patch addressing security vulnerabilities along with other reported issues. The patch can be distributed through Veeam’s update mechanisms or installed using updated installation media. After upgrading, administrators should verify that the expected fixed build is running. They should also confirm that backup and replication jobs operate normally and test restoration capabilities. Security updates to backup infrastructure should not be considered complete until recoverability has been validated. Because no vulnerability-specific exploit indicators are currently public, organizations should review historical activity on systems that remained vulnerable before patching. Important sources include: Veeam service logs Windows Event Logs Veeam configuration and job history EDR telemetry from backup servers Firewall and network flow logs Authentication records Administrative activity vCenter and virtualization management logs Security teams should investigate unexpected changes to jobs, repositories, replication configuration, protection policies, infrastructure components, or administrative accounts. Backup integrity should also be verified. Attackers frequently target backup systems during broader intrusions to impair recovery. Even though public reporting does not establish ransomware exploitation of this CVE, organizations investigating suspicious activity should confirm that restore points, immutable copies, and offline backups have not been altered. Where compromise cannot be excluded, incident responders should protect clean backup copies before conducting remediation. Credentials accessible from the backup infrastructure should also be reviewed and rotated if evidence indicates unauthorized access. Organizations running Veeam Agent for Linux managed by Backup & Replication should separately upgrade vulnerable agents to version 13.1.2, build 13.1.2.11, to remediate CVE-2026-105477. The critical authorization bypass and the three additional vulnerabilities were reported to Veeam through HackerOne. Veeam released fixes for all four issues on October 27, 2026. Disclaimer: Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. Veeam has released security updates to address CVE-2026-108142, a critical authorization bypass vulnerability affecting Veeam Backup & Replication 13. The flaw allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass authorization controls associated with the Veeam CDP Coordinator Service.

The vulnerability carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.1 and affects both Windows-based Veeam Backup & Replication deployments and the Veeam Software Appliance. Veeam disclosed the issue on October 27, 2026 as part of security advisory KB4948.

Backup infrastructure is an especially sensitive security target because it contains recovery data and often has privileged connectivity to production systems. An authorization weakness affecting a central backup component therefore warrants immediate attention even though the vendor has not publicly documented the complete exploitation chain.

Veeam’s CVSS vector identifies network-based exploitation with low attack complexity, no privileges required, and no user interaction. However, the vector also specifies that additional attack requirements must be present. Veeam has not publicly explained those prerequisites.

The vulnerability affects Veeam Backup & Replication 13.1.1.18 and all earlier builds in the 13.1 branch, as well as version 13.0.2.29 and all earlier 13.0 builds. Veeam explicitly states that older releases such as version 12.x are not affected by this specific flaw.

For CVE-2026-108142 detection, security teams should prioritize identifying vulnerable Backup & Replication installations and monitoring the backup server for unexpected activity involving the CDP Coordinator Service, unauthorized configuration changes, suspicious backup infrastructure modifications, and network connections from untrusted systems.

SOC Prime users can strengthen visibility into vulnerability exploitation and post-compromise activity by correlating network, endpoint, identity, and application telemetry with behavior-based detection content.

Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and hunting logic. To Detect CVE-2026-108142, defenders should combine vulnerability inventory with monitoring of Veeam services, administrative activity, system changes, and network access to backup infrastructure.

Contact Sales

CVE-2026-108142 analysis

The vulnerability is located in the Veeam CDP Coordinator Service, a component of Veeam Backup & Replication responsible for coordinating Continuous Data Protection operations.

According to Veeam documentation, the CDP Coordinator Service runs on the backup server and communicates with VMware vCenter, assigns CDP tasks, manages infrastructure components involved in Continuous Data Protection, and coordinates replication and data transfer operations.

This makes authorization controls around the service particularly important. The backup server acts as the configuration and management core of the backup infrastructure, while the CDP Coordinator Service can interact with infrastructure components involved in replication.

The details for CVE-2026-108142 remain intentionally limited in the public disclosure.

Veeam describes the vulnerability as allowing an unauthenticated attacker to bypass authorization on the CDP Coordinator Service but does not disclose the vulnerable request, affected function, protocol interaction, exploitation sequence, or underlying implementation defect.

The CVE is categorized as CWE-636, Not Failing Securely, commonly described as a “fail-open” condition. This weakness class occurs when a security mechanism encounters an error or unexpected state and falls into a less secure condition instead of denying access.

However, the CWE classification alone should not be used to infer the precise implementation error in Veeam’s software. The vendor has not published enough technical information to determine exactly how the authorization bypass is triggered.

The CVSS v4.0 vector is:

CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:H/SA:H

This indicates:

  • Network-based attack vector
  • Low attack complexity
  • Additional attack requirements present
  • No privileges required
  • No user interaction required
  • No direct confidentiality impact identified
  • High integrity and availability impact
  • High integrity and availability impact on subsequent systems

That final distinction is important. Veeam’s scoring suggests that successful exploitation could affect not only the vulnerable backup system but also systems downstream from it. However, the vendor has not described exactly what operations an attacker can perform after bypassing authorization.

Neither Veeam nor the supplied reports state that the vulnerability provides arbitrary remote code execution.

CybersecurityNews specifically notes that the advisory does not describe an attack sequence or say that the flaw enables RCE. CyberPress likewise states that Veeam has not published exploitation steps or claimed code execution.

Therefore, claims that the flaw directly provides shell access, SYSTEM privileges, credential theft, or arbitrary command execution would currently go beyond the available evidence.

CVE-2026-108142 affects two Veeam Backup & Replication 13 branches:

  • Version 13.1.1.18 and earlier 13.1 builds
  • Version 13.0.2.29 and earlier 13.0 builds

The vulnerability applies to both Windows-based Veeam Backup & Replication installations and Veeam Software Appliance deployments.

Veeam Backup & Replication 12.x and other older releases identified by the vendor are not affected by this particular issue.

Organizations should verify the exact build rather than relying solely on the major version number.

For example, an installation reporting version 13.1 may still be vulnerable unless it has been upgraded to build 13.1.2.57 or later.

Administrators can review their installed Backup & Replication build from the product interface and compare it with Veeam’s release information.

At the time of writing, no public CVE-2026-108142 PoC has been documented by Veeam or the supplied security reports. Independent public vulnerability tracking also reports no openly available proof-of-concept exploit.

Veeam has likewise not reported active exploitation of the vulnerability.

This distinction is particularly relevant because Veeam infrastructure has been targeted through other vulnerabilities in previous attacks. CybersecurityNews notes prior exploitation of CVE-2024-40711 in ransomware operations, but that historical activity does not demonstrate exploitation of the newly disclosed authorization bypass.

As of October 29, 2026, the new CVE is also not listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog according to currently available vulnerability tracking data.

There are therefore no confirmed campaign-specific CVE-2026-108142 IOCs such as malicious IP addresses, domains, hashes, exploit payloads, or known attacker infrastructure associated with this vulnerability.

Security teams should instead focus on exposure assessment and behavioral monitoring.

Potential investigation points include:

  • Network connections to Veeam backup infrastructure from unexpected systems
  • Unexpected interaction with the CDP Coordinator Service
  • Unauthorized changes to backup or CDP configuration
  • New or modified backup jobs without an administrative explanation
  • Unexpected service restarts or failures
  • Changes to replication policies
  • Modifications to protected infrastructure that do not correspond with approved administrative activity
  • Suspicious account or privilege changes on the backup server
  • Unexpected processes or network activity originating from Veeam infrastructure
  • Attempts to reach backup management services from user networks or internet-facing systems

These behaviors are not vulnerability-specific indicators. They are defensive hunting opportunities that may help uncover suspicious activity involving a critical backup server while technical exploitation details remain unavailable.

Organizations should also review network segmentation around Veeam infrastructure.

Backup servers should not be broadly reachable from ordinary workstations, guest environments, or untrusted network segments. Only systems that require communication with Veeam services should be permitted to reach the relevant interfaces and ports.

This reduces the number of systems capable of interacting with a vulnerable service while patches are being deployed.

The October security update also addresses three additional vulnerabilities.

CVE-2026-108140 and CVE-2026-108141 are medium-severity relative path traversal vulnerabilities rated CVSS 5.9. Exploitation requires an authenticated Restore Operator who also controls the contents of a backed-up NAS share. Under those conditions, attacker-controlled files can be written to arbitrary locations on the backup server.

A separate issue, CVE-2026-105477, affects Veeam Agent for Linux installations managed by Backup & Replication. The high-severity vulnerability can enable local privilege escalation and is fixed in Veeam Agent for Linux 13.1.2, build 13.1.2.11.

Organizations applying the October updates should therefore review their entire Veeam environment rather than addressing only the critical authorization bypass.

CVE-2026-108142 Mitigation

The primary remediation is to install the fixed Veeam Backup & Replication releases.

For the 13.1 branch, upgrade to:

Veeam Backup & Replication 13.1.2 — build 13.1.2.57

For the 13.0 branch, upgrade to:

Veeam Backup & Replication 13.0.3 — build 13.0.3.63

These builds contain the vendor-provided fix for the authorization vulnerability.

The recommended CVE-2026-108142 mitigation process should begin with identifying every Veeam Backup & Replication server and determining its exact installed build.

Security teams should prioritize upgrades for backup servers that are accessible across large network segments, connected to critical virtualization infrastructure, or supporting high-value production workloads.

The patch should be treated as a security priority because exploitation requires no authenticated account according to the published CVSS vector.

Veeam has not published a complete workaround in KB4948 that eliminates the vulnerability without installing the fixed software.

If an immediate upgrade is operationally impossible, organizations should apply defense-in-depth measures until patching can be completed:

  • Restrict access to Veeam backup servers using network segmentation.
  • Permit connections only from systems that legitimately require access.
  • Block unnecessary communication from workstation and user VLANs.
  • Prevent direct internet exposure of backup infrastructure.
  • Apply host-based firewall restrictions where operationally appropriate.
  • Monitor access to Veeam services from unexpected systems.
  • Review administrative and backup configuration changes.
  • Monitor the backup server for unusual process execution or outbound connections.
  • Protect administrative credentials using strong authentication and least privilege.
  • Maintain immutable or offline backup copies where possible.

These controls reduce attack surface but should not be considered substitutes for the vendor update.

Veeam’s release information states that 13.1.2.57 is a cumulative patch addressing security vulnerabilities along with other reported issues. The patch can be distributed through Veeam’s update mechanisms or installed using updated installation media.

After upgrading, administrators should verify that the expected fixed build is running.

They should also confirm that backup and replication jobs operate normally and test restoration capabilities. Security updates to backup infrastructure should not be considered complete until recoverability has been validated.

Because no vulnerability-specific exploit indicators are currently public, organizations should review historical activity on systems that remained vulnerable before patching.

Important sources include:

  • Veeam service logs
  • Windows Event Logs
  • Veeam configuration and job history
  • EDR telemetry from backup servers
  • Firewall and network flow logs
  • Authentication records
  • Administrative activity
  • vCenter and virtualization management logs

Security teams should investigate unexpected changes to jobs, repositories, replication configuration, protection policies, infrastructure components, or administrative accounts.

Backup integrity should also be verified.

Attackers frequently target backup systems during broader intrusions to impair recovery. Even though public reporting does not establish ransomware exploitation of this CVE, organizations investigating suspicious activity should confirm that restore points, immutable copies, and offline backups have not been altered.

Where compromise cannot be excluded, incident responders should protect clean backup copies before conducting remediation.

Credentials accessible from the backup infrastructure should also be reviewed and rotated if evidence indicates unauthorized access.

Organizations running Veeam Agent for Linux managed by Backup & Replication should separately upgrade vulnerable agents to version 13.1.2, build 13.1.2.11, to remediate CVE-2026-105477.

The critical authorization bypass and the three additional vulnerabilities were reported to Veeam through HackerOne. Veeam released fixes for all four issues on October 27, 2026.

items.title: Closing the loop: Why an effective SOC focuses on remediation, not just containment
items.summary: By Oliver Spence, CEO, CybaVerse According to a recent report from insurance firm Hiscox, 38 percent of UK organisations have a suffered cyber attack in the last year. The figure is not hugely surprising. Cyber crime is widely recognised as the number one threat to business today. However, what is concerning is that the rate of attacks is surging even despite organisations increasing their spending on defences. According to the same study, firms are spending significant money to ward off the threat of hacks, with the average UK firm spending £44,294 on resilience measures. This raises an important question, why when organisations are boosting their investments in cyber defences are business crippling attacks continuing to surge? The UK’s outsourced security market UK organisations spend heavily on outsourced cyber security. Government analysis recently revealed that the cyber services market, which includes MSSPs, is now worth approximately £8.4 billion annually. The figure highlights that many organisations in the UK are outsourcing their security, ensuring it is managed by experts. This is also not surprising. Cyber security is a full-time, 24/7 position and most organisations don’t have the resources to manage it internally. However, even despite this migration to managed services, it doesn’t explain why operationally impacting attacks continue to increase? Could it highlight that traditional managed security models are often too focused on identifying threats, rather than helping organisations actually remove the weaknesses that allow threats to succeed? Managed Detection and Response One of the most common activities for organisations to outsource is their security operations. Organisations will rely on experts to monitor their digital assets for malicious activity, ensuring incidents are stopped and contained before they escalate into full scale attacks. However, one of the key issues with Managed Detection and Response is that it only focuses on containment, not remediation. Security analysts will continually triage alerts coming into the SOC, investigating them to identify malicious activity. If malicious activity occurs, they will then work to understand the incident, investigate it and contain it. However, this model only contains the incident, it doesn’t remediate the cause behind it. Take the exploitation of an unpatched vulnerability. A SOC may detect the malicious activity, isolate the affected device, remove malicious files and restore the environment to its previous state. The incident has been contained, but has the problem actually been remediated? Not if the vulnerability remains unpatched. The same applies if an attacker gained access because of a misconfiguration, weak Microsoft 365 control or another security gap. Restoring the environment to the state it was in before the attack simply restores the weakness too. This is where we need to make a much clearer distinction between containment and remediation. Containment stops the immediate threat. Remediation addresses the weakness that allowed it to happen in the first place. Without the final step, organisations risk operating in permanent firefighting mode. The flames are extinguished, but nobody is addressing what keeps starting the fires. Introducing MDR+R When organisations are selecting an MDR provider, they first must understand the genuine improvements to security being offered. Simply acting on incidents is not enough. The partner must also make tangible improvements to the overall security of the business. One of the best ways to achieve this is by partnering with providers that don’t just respond to threats, but also take actions to remediate the root cause of incidents. These providers don’t simply triage alerts and contain incidents, they work to understand how an attack happened and then provide support to organisations to remediate the issue at its very root. The overall goal is to close the loop on incidents, not leave them open to be exploited again. The three-year test This brings us to a question every organisation outsourcing its security should ask. If you have been working with a SOC provider for three years, are you more secure today than you were when the relationship started? Your attack surface may have expanded. Threat activity may have increased. Attackers may have become more sophisticated. These factors obviously won’t be within your SOC provider’s control, but there should still be tangible evidence that security is improving. Known weaknesses should be getting closed. Previously identified attack paths should be disappearing. Misconfigurations should be addressed. Vulnerabilities should be remediated. The number of exploitable gaps sitting within the environment should be reducing. If, after three years, and significant investment, the same security gaps remain open, organisations have every right to ask what they are paying for. Containment keeps an organisation running. Remediation makes it more secure. Organisations must demand both.
